articles.title: Crypto hacks surge 55% to $1.2B, but key theft drops by 30%
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Hacken recorded $1.18 billion in Q3 theft across 107 incidents, reporting a 55% rise from Q2.
- Hacken's published shares imply about 30% lower operational losses, a comparison constrained by rounded figures and broad categories.
- Bitget and Liquid illustrate different withdrawal failures, supporting checks on both authorization and asset validity.
Hacken's third-quarter crypto hack total rose to $1.18 billion while the losses implied by its access-control and operational figures fell about 30%.
The crypto security firm's Oct. 15 disclosure reports a 55% increase in total theft for July-September compared with the second quarter.
The change included 48% more losses from smart contracts in the third quarter, up from about 11% in Hacken's original second-quarter summary. More incidents, alongside a slightly smaller mean recorded loss per incident, also distinguish the two quarters. The figures challenge a fixed security hierarchy that makes custody operations the overriding priority.
Bitget's September report showed forged withdrawal instructions without private-key compromise, while Liquid's report from the same month accepted invalid assets before a genuine authorization process released Bitcoin against them.
What changed across Hacken's quarters
Hacken's second-quarter summary recorded $763.9 million extracted across 67 incidents, attributing 88.3% of losses to compromised keys, signers, and infrastructure.
Multiplying those figures gives approximately $675 million, while applying the 40% share for the third quarter to $1.18 billion gives approximately $472 million, about 30% less.
The third-quarter report calls its category access-control and operational failures, while the second-quarter report describes operational failures.
The third-quarter 48% share implies about $566 million, compared with roughly $84 million using the second-quarter original 11% share.
That discrepancy, rounded inputs, and uncertain detailed category comparability rule out a precise growth multiple, but the published mix points to much heavier contract losses.
The overall increase also looks different when separated into incident frequency and average severity. Recorded incidents rose from 67 to 107, so dividing the published totals by those counts gives an arithmetic mean of roughly $11.4 million in the second quarter and $11 million in the third quarter. More incidents can lift an aggregate even when the arithmetic mean falls.
Hacken attributed 75.5% of the second-quarter losses to just two incidents, at Drift Protocol and KelpDAO. Smart contract bugs appeared in 44 of that quarter's 67 incidents while accounting for only about 11% of lost value.
A falling category total can coexist with frequent failures and continued potential for severe losses. Establishing improved controls would require comparable exposure and evidence of which safeguards held or failed.
A category's share of past damage helps explain a period, while its importance to a particular institution depends on that institution's exposure and control processes.
How Bitget and Liquid lost control of crypto withdrawals
Bitget's Sept. 30 investigation update said compromised third-party security products enabled unauthorized access to its exchange wallet environment in the Sept. 24 incident.
Its account update on Oct. 14 describes attackers obtaining high-privilege internal credentials and injecting forged withdrawal commands.
Bitget says private-key compromise was ruled out and cold wallets were unaffected. The exchange says compromised privileged credentials nevertheless enabled forged withdrawal instructions. That finding distinguishes the signing key from the processes allowed to request its use.
This is an operational authorization problem, and the question is how a withdrawal request earns permission to move funds, including what the system accepts as trusted internal activity. A custody design can protect the key while still allowing a compromised upstream process to ask for the wrong transfer.
Bitget's initial notice estimated approximately $351.6 million affected, and its Sept. 25 update raised that to about $387.5 million after including additional assets. The October account puts the final verified affected amount at approximately $388 million.
Bitget attributes those revisions to fuller accounting of the original unauthorized transfers. The revisions describe the original Sept. 24 transfers more completely, and illustrate how an initial crypto theft estimate and an eventual net loss can answer different questions.
In its Sept. 23 assessment, Blockstream said an Elements range-proof cache defect allowed approximately 4,000 unbacked liquid staking token LBTC to pass validation.
In effect, nodes reused a record of a successful check for a transaction that should have failed. Blockstream traced the defect to a cache-bug fix that added missing fields without unambiguous length framing.
Different arrangements of the fields could produce the same input bytes, allowing an invalid proof to reuse a cached valid result.
SideSwap, which processed the peg-out converting LBTC into BTC, acknowledged that it handled the roughly 4,000-LBTC order automatically without size, velocity, or wallet-history checks. It said online keys and automatic forwarding removed a manual opportunity to hold the released Bitcoin.
Blockstream said the peg-out authorization key was not stolen or forged, and the authorization operated on assets the network had already incorrectly accepted. SideSwap likewise said no key, wallet or system of its own was compromised.
The sequence crossed two security boundaries: whether the assets were valid and whether they could be released. A pause, limit or review in the withdrawal process could have provided another opportunity to interrupt the transfer after validation failed.
Liquid's outcome depended on both the validation defect that created the assets and the operational process that let Bitcoin leave.
Recovered funds and protected balances answer different questions
Blockstream's September assessment recorded 3,400 BTC returned on Sept. 7 and approximately 602 BTC outstanding at the report date.
Bitget says user balances were unaffected, its Protection Fund covers the incident's financial impact, and phased withdrawals reopened on Oct. 2. Those statements, in its Oct. 14 account update, address customer balances, financial coverage, and service access.
Bitget makes the integrity of withdrawal instructions central. Liquid makes asset validation central, while SideSwap's role shows why operational checkpoints still matter after validation fails. Together, they support testing the full path from an asset's validity to permission to release it.
New quarterly mix adds another constraint: an institution cannot choose its most important safeguard from the previous quarter's largest loss category alone. The practical question is which independent checkpoints can interrupt the release path when an earlier safeguard fails.

articles.title: Abandoned Bitcoin? Wallet Targeted by Noah Doe Lawsuit Moves $33 Million - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- An address first funded in September 2013 moved 411.45 BTC, worth about $33.4 million, to a new wallet on Sunday, its first outgoing transfer ever.
- The coins cost about $54,000 when Bitcoin traded near $130, and the transfer went to an unlabeled address, not an exchange.
- Galaxy tagged the address as one of 39,069 named in a New York lawsuit by “Noah Doe” seeking ownership of dormant wallets as abandoned property.
Another long-sleeping Bitcoin whale has stirred, and this one is named in a lawsuit claiming its coins were abandoned.
An address beginning with "13Coop" that had never sent a single coin since it was first funded on Sept. 11, 2013, moved 411.45 BTC, worth roughly $33.4 million, on Sunday, according to Galaxy Research. Arkham data shows the coins landed in a single new address, where they remain.
When the wallet was funded, Bitcoin traded around $130, according to Arkham, meaning the stash cost about $54,000. Galaxy put the holder’s average cost basis near $127 and the paper gain at more than 64,000%. It’s unclear whether the owner plans to sell, since the transfer went to an unlabeled address, not an exchange.
Galaxy tagged the sending address as “Noah Doe #970,” marking it as one of 39,069 dormant addresses named in a New York lawsuit filed this year by a pseudonymous plaintiff called Noah Doe and two Wyoming companies.
🏚️ 💤 Address awakened — dormant 13+ years — 411.45 BTC sent
This address had never sent coins (first funded 2013-09-11, 13.1y ago); it just spent 411.45 BTC ($33.44M) in block 972,036
Address: 13Coop8xFbYj9JR9WyF5EqzGa9GiZmxs7C
Coins moved: 411.45 BTC in 2 UTXOs — all held…
— Galaxy Research (@glxyresearch) October 18, 2026
The plaintiffs argue that the wallets, which hold about 3.8 million BTC, qualify as abandoned property under the state’s lost-and-found law, even though they hold none of the private keys.
Galaxy also flagged the address as one of those “dusted” in a 2025 campaign that sent tiny amounts of Bitcoin carrying embedded messages to dormant wallets, which Galaxy has described as groundwork for the abandonment claim. Arkham’s data shows a string of those dust deposits, some labeled as phishing.
Each move chips away at the lawsuit’s premise. Spending coins requires the private keys, which suggests at least some of the targeted wallets are anything but abandoned. Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn has said the pace of dormant “Noah Doe” coins moving onchain has been accelerating month over month.
The wallet joins a growing list of old coins on the move. Bitcoin’s oldest coins have been waking up at an unusual clip in 2026, according to Galaxy Research data.
Just a little over a week ago, a Satoshi-era wallet mined in 2010 moved for the first time in 16 years. In late September, about $161 million in decade-old Bitcoin was transferred over the course of roughly two weeks. And just last week, a whale moved a whopping $377 million after holding through every major market crash since 2020.

articles.title: Hoskinson reveals new code for Cardano, but $63M TVL exposes a gap
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Hoskinson is building a new Cardano programming language as he declares that the upcoming Leios upgrade will complete his original blockchain vision.
- Cardano's modest financial activity contrasts with Solana's 90-fold DeFi lead, underscoring the challenge of converting technical advances into adoption.
- With Leios still awaiting deployment and no launch date for the new language, Cardano faces a critical test of whether its upgrades can stimulate demand.
Charles Hoskinson is developing a new programming language for Cardano as the blockchain approaches a pivotal test of commercial demand.
The Cardano founder said he is working with developer Lucas Rosa, a software engineer at Input Output Global, on a language supporting intent-based transactions and proof-carrying data using Groth16 cryptographic proofs.
The announcement follows Hoskinson's declaration that the forthcoming Leios scalability upgrade would complete his original vision for the blockchain, marking a potential turning point after years of technical development.
The ambitions contrast with Cardano's economic footprint. Despite its ADA token commanding a market capitalization of about $8.3 billion, decentralized finance applications on the network hold just $63 million in assets, while daily trading volume remains below $1 million.
The disparity raises questions about whether additional technology can attract the users and capital needed to support a larger financial ecosystem.
Cardano's limited liquidity raises stakes for its next upgrade
According to DefiLlama, Cardano's decentralized exchanges processed approximately $927,000 in transactions over the preceding 24 hours as of Oct. 19. Weekly trading volume stood at $8.35 million, down 25% from the previous seven-day period.
The network also recorded 12,716 active addresses and 28,146 transactions during the day, generating approximately $2,196 in blockchain fees. Its stablecoin supply stood at about $70 million, reflecting a relatively small pool of dollar-denominated liquidity to support trading, lending, and other financial applications.
The figures stand out when compared with larger blockchain ecosystems.
For example, Solana held approximately $5.9 billion in DeFi deposits and processed $1.45 billion in decentralized exchange transactions over the same 24-hour period, according to DefiLlama. Its stablecoin supply exceeded $15.5 billion.
Although Solana's market capitalization stands at roughly $62 billion, about seven times Cardano's, its DeFi deposits are more than 90 times larger, showing how unevenly capital and financial activity are distributed among competing blockchain networks.
For Cardano, that gap creates a commercial challenge extending beyond transaction-processing capacity.
Decentralized exchanges need sufficient liquidity to accommodate larger trades without significant price slippage, while lending platforms require deposits and borrowing demand to generate revenue. Limited activity can make it harder for developers to sustain applications, reducing the incentive for additional capital to enter the ecosystem.
Hoskinson's completion claim comes as Cardano attempts to overcome another longstanding constraint through Ouroboros Leios, an upgrade designed to substantially increase the number of transactions the blockchain can process.
The project's development roadmap targets 10 to 65 times throughput improvements through a phased implementation, potentially enabling Cardano to support far more demanding applications.
Hoskinson described Leios as the final component of his original vision, which includes decentralized consensus and governance, the extended unspent transaction output accounting model, Plutus smart contracts, formal verification and multiple independent node implementations.
The upgrade would give Cardano greater processing capacity. Still, its relatively modest transaction volumes suggest that expanding demand for the network may prove just as consequential as increasing its technical limits.
That places greater attention on Hoskinson's latest programming language initiative and whether it can make the blockchain more attractive to developers building sophisticated financial applications.
New programming language opens another front in adoption push
The upcoming language could change how applications are designed and run on Cardano.
Intent-based systems let users specify the outcome they want from a transaction, while software executes it under predefined conditions. For financial applications, this could simplify operations involving multiple asset exchanges, automated execution, and complex settlement requirements.
Proof-carrying data adds another capability by attaching cryptographic evidence to information to support its validity. Combined with Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs, this could enable applications to verify certain transactions or computations without exposing all the underlying information.
The approach could support financial products that require automated settlement, confidential verification, and more sophisticated interactions between decentralized services.
Hoskinson described the proposed language as the first of its kind, though it has not yet published its architecture, performance characteristics, or technical specifications.
Lucas Rosa's involvement is significant because he previously helped develop Aiken, a programming language designed to make building smart contracts on Cardano more accessible.
Aiken was developed to simplify a process historically associated with Plutus and its Haskell-based programming environment. Its compiler, testing tools, and more familiar syntax were intended to lower the technical barriers facing developers entering the ecosystem.
The new project could extend that effort into intent-based execution and cryptographic verification, areas that may become increasingly relevant as decentralized applications incorporate automated trading and autonomous software agents.
Cardano already supports cryptographic primitives that can verify pairing-based zero-knowledge proofs, so the proposed language's commercial appeal will depend partly on how effectively it packages those capabilities for developers.
That raises an immediate question about adoption. Improved developer tools can reduce the cost and complexity of launching applications, but developers also need access to users, liquidity, and transaction demand to make their products commercially sustainable.

articles.title: Bitcoin Tests Key Support as Oil and AI Fears Squeeze Markets - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Bitcoin trades at $82,164, just above the a key support line, after touching $83,040 today and giving back part of the gain.
- Oil near $108, 3.7% inflation, and a 10-year yield above 5% keep rate-hike fears alive, while spot Bitcoin ETFs lost about $910 million in two weeks.
- Technical indicators on the charts suggest caution for traders in the near term.
Bitcoin continues to defy seasonal ‘Uptober” expectations, as macroeconomic factors weigh heavily on the digital asset.
Bitcoin is hovering around $82,000 on Monday, up about 1% on the day, after tagging $83,000 early and handing some of it back.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, trades near $108 a barrel after weekend attacks on Persian Gulf tankers and Russian crude facilities. Pricey oil raises the cost of fuel and freight, which feeds inflation. The consumer price index (CPI), what households pay, rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, while the producer price index (PPI), what businesses pay, jumped 6.3%, the biggest annual rise since 2022.
That likely pushes the Federal Reserve toward raising interest rates, which makes borrowing costlier. Markets see roughly a 15% chance of a quarter-point hike next week. You can see it in Treasury yields, the return investors earn lending to the U.S. government: when hike bets rise, bond prices fall and yields climb. The 10-year sits at 5.08% and the 2-year at 4.72%, CNBC data shows.
A near risk-free 5% competes with stocks and crypto for the same money, and it raises the debt costs of the AI giants that borrowed heavily for data centers. Bitcoin trades with that risk basket, so AI selloffs tend to drag it down.
The pain was concentrated in companies paying for the AI buildout with borrowed money. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% on Friday and closed its worst week since June, with AMD down 6% and Micron down 5.6% on the day. CoreWeave, a so-called “neocloud” that rents out AI computing power, lost about 24% over the week, and it funds much of its data center spending with debt and new share sales rather than cash flow.
Hotter inflation and higher yields make that kind of debt costlier to carry, so the stock selloff and the bond market are really the same story.
Bitcoin price: technical analysis
Bitcoin trades at $82,164 on the daily chart, up 0.18% in today’s forming candlestick, sitting right on the 0.236 Fibonacci retracement at $81,603. Fibonacci levels mark where pullbacks tend to pause, and 23.6% is the shallowest, so holding it keeps the climb from the $87,422 high intact. The bounce is weak, though: a week of small candle bodies says neither side is in control.
Bitcoin’s current price is also inside the $81,847 to $82,305 "golden zone" of the recent $80,365 to $84,246 swing, where buyers often show up.
The 50-day exponential moving average, or EMA, weights recent prices more heavily and sits at about $80,548, above the 200-day EMA at about $75,932, with current price above both. That formation, known as golden cross, reads bullish because short-term buyers are paying more than long-term holders.
The Average Directional Index, or ADX, measures trend strength, and currently reads 21.6. Below 25 means no firm trend and more false breakouts. The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, is at 49.3, basically dead neutral with neither bulls nor bears dominating the market.
So, without a clear trend, the Squeeze Momentum Indicator has been "on" for 13 days, meaning volatility is compressed like a spring. Momentum at -1.42 leans mildly down.
A daily close below $81,603 opens $81,196 and the 50-day EMA. Bulls need closes above $83,330 and $84,246, ideally with a rising ADX. The Fed meeting next week and major earnings calls (like Meta and Tesla) this week are the next catalysts to follow.

articles.title: Bitcoin Weekly Close Slips From Support Zone as Tech Stocks Eye Recovery
articles.text:
Stocks rebound into key tech earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week
Analysts expect Bitcoin to retest $80,000 support again as stock markets attempt to recover last week’s losses.
Bitcoin (BTC) starts the third week of October at $82,000 as crypto and stock markets begin a tentative rebound.
Key points:
- South Korea’s KOSPI Composite Index gained nearly 1.8% on Monday after last week’s tech-driven losses.
- Markets have priced out two further interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve in 2026, seeing 75% odds of only one 25-basis-point hike by the end of the year.
- Bitcoin delivered a weekly close below key local support after the Coinbase Premium Index hit -0.14, its lowest level since late June.
Asia leads equities bounce ahead of tech earnings
A lighter week of US macro data prints will shift the market’s attention to corporate earnings as stocks rebound from last week’s sell-off. Some 15% of S&P 500 companies are due to report third-quarter earnings figures this week, including SpaceX on Tuesday and Tesla and Meta on Wednesday.
Tech-stock performance remains in focus after a major drawdown last week that began with South Korean markets. The KOSPI Composite Index lost 2.8% on Oct. 12 before dropping to the week’s low of 5,455 on Thursday, bringing the week-to-date losses temporarily to 17%.
KOSPI Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Contagion spread to neighboring Asian markets before US equities began to weaken later in the week. The S&P 500 index finished Friday down 2% for the week.
As in early August, tech stocks saw considerable sell-side pressure amid concerns over AI expenditure plans and the associated debt obligations. In Korea, the threat of competition in semiconductor manufacturing from China exacerbated the downturn.
Warnings of a “Black Monday” event on global stock markets spread through social media over the weekend. The panic, which coincided with the 39th anniversary of the 1987 Black Monday crash, appeared misplaced, with KOSPI gaining 1.8% on Monday and S&P 500 futures 0.7% higher at the time of writing.
S&P 500 futures one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Commenting on the disconnect between public sentiment and market performance, market commentator The Kobeissi Letter suggested that stocks should outperform based on investor demand. Persistent high US inflation and a global energy crisis have positioned equities for a surge on any potential signs of conditions improving.
“All while the AI Revolution continues to accelerate and many large-cap technology stocks become cheaper on a forward earnings basis, even as their stock prices rise. And in the background, the demand for asset ownership is historically robust,” it summarized in analysis last week.
Kobeissi noted that while tech giants led S&P 500 strength, 80% of index stocks are trading at least 10% below all-time highs.
Fed rate-hike bets cool despite inflation data overshoot
Ahead of the Federal Reserve’s next decision on interest-rate changes on Oct. 28, markets have tempered their expectations on policy tightening.
Data from CME Group’s FedWatch Tool shows 85% odds of rates staying within their current 3.75-4.00% range in October. The Fed’s December meeting, meanwhile, carries just 11% odds of a further pause. Instead, markets see a 75% chance of a 25-basis-point hike, with a 50-basis-point move attracting 13% odds.
Fed target-rate probabilities (screenshot). Source: CME Group
In a discussion with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva last week, Fed chair Kevin Warsh avoided any hints of forward guidance on policy, reinforcing a pledge made at the Jackson Hole economic symposium in August.
“I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” he said.
Markets, however, interpreted the lack of information as a dovish signal, doubling down on the Fed hiking rates just once more before 2027.
Adopting a cautionary tone, meanwhile, market commentator Mosaic Asset Company saw inflation trends forcing the Fed to avoid easing off, keeping a crypto and risk-asset headwind in place.
“While investors expect the Federal Reserve to hold rates steady at its next meeting later this month, a growing inflation problem will keep favoring tighter monetary policy,” it wrote in analysis on Sunday.
The September print of the US Producer Price Index (PPI) released last week showed the ongoing impact of the Middle East crisis on fuel prices. PPI delivered its largest month-on-month increase since March 2022 at 1.7%.
“Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3%,” the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.
Fuel also accounted for more than half of the September increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which beat expectations by 0.1% to hit 3.7% year-on-year.
Related: Bitcoin, Ether ETFs shed $549M as October ETH outflows near $1B
BTC price analysis sees more $80,000 support retests
Bitcoin price action completed a weekly candle close below a key support zone of interest between $82,500 and $82,800.
The weekly close came in at $82,000, a move that crypto trader and analyst Rekt Capital warned could spark further retests of the $80,000 mark in the future.
“Such a Weekly Close would position Bitcoin for a potential bearish retest of ~$82500 into new resistance. And if that bearish retest occurs successfully then it could set price up for a drop below $80k within the next few weeks,” he wrote in analysis on X.
BTC/USD one-week chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Previously, Cointelegraph reported on September’s local high near $87,000 now hosting multiple resistance components, including the 2026 yearly open and its 20-month simple moving average (SMA).
In its latest market overview, onchain analytics platform CryptoQuant flagged declining US investor demand as a reemerging BTC price headwind this month. The Coinbase Premium Index, which measures the difference in price between Coinbase’s and Binance’s BTC/USDT pairs, fell to -0.141 on Oct. 18, its lowest levels since June 30.
“This reading is particularly significant. If the index remains in negative territory, it could indicate insufficient demand to absorb selling pressure, potentially increasing the likelihood of a continued price correction in the short term,” CryptoQuant commented.
Coinbase Premium Index. Source: CryptoQuant
The lack of demand contrasts with BTC/USD holding gains made since the end of June, having bounced from new multiyear lows under $58,000 on July 1.

articles.title: JPMorgan Expands JPM Coin to Ethereum for Institutions
articles.text:
JPMorgan takes JPM Coin to Ethereum for institutional clients: Report
JPMorgan is reportedly expanding its JPM Coin deposit token to Ethereum, allowing institutional clients to make payments and settle tokenized asset transactions.
JPMorgan Chase, the world’s biggest bank by market capitalization, is expanding its JPM Coin deposit token to Ethereum, Bloomberg reported on Monday.
JPM Coin represents US dollar deposits held at JPMorgan and lets eligible clients transfer funds within seconds, around the clock.
Emma Landriault, global head of Kinexys Labs, said crypto companies could use the token for blockchain payments, while financial institutions could use it to settle trades and post collateral.
Landriault said JPMorgan chose Ethereum for its liquidity and existing use among clients. While the tokens are issued on public networks, JPM Coin will remain restricted to approved institutional participants.
The expansion follows JPMorgan’s November 2025 rollout of JPM Coin on Base, an Ethereum layer-2 network built by cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase. At the time, JPMorgan said it planned to support additional public blockchains. In January, JPMorgan announced plans to bring JPM Coin to the Canton Network.
Cointelegraph contacted JPMorgan for additional details but did not receive an immediate response.
Related: Argentine banks testing JPMorgan’s JPM Coin to speed up settlements: Report

articles.title: Kraken’s opt-in European wallet can expose spot holdings to futures losses
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Kraken’s EEA Unified Wallet rollout lets eligible Kraken Pro users pool collateral after manually activating the setting.
- Default cross margin can expose the full eligible pool, including qualifying spot and Earn balances, to a losing futures position.
- Isolated margin covers linear Multi-M futures; switching back to separate wallets requires closing derivatives positions and active orders.
Kraken’s Unified Wallet rollout to eligible European Economic Area clients can expose crypto held for spot trading and qualifying Earn balances to futures losses after users switch it on. Its default cross-margin setting allows a losing position to draw on the account’s entire eligible balance.
The exchange announced EEA availability on October 16, 2026. Unified Wallet combines eligible spot, margin, Earn and futures balances on Kraken Pro, removing the need to transfer collateral into a separate futures wallet.
The announcement includes eligible Earn balances without identifying every qualifying product. Kraken’s wallet guide, which describes the default wallet setup, distinguishes active staking and Earn strategies held in an Earn wallet from Auto Earn balances remaining in Main.
Activation is manual through Kraken Pro’s account settings, with eligible balances pooled immediately afterward. Futures trading must also be enabled. Kraken’s EEA derivatives requirements include account verification and, for new futures clients, a knowledge-and-experience questionnaire and a tax identification number.
Kraken says more than 40 cryptocurrencies, alongside USD, EUR and gold (XAU), can serve as collateral.
In cross-margin mode, margin is calculated across the eligible pool. A loss can therefore reach spot holdings that would remain separate from futures losses under the separate-wallet arrangement, according to Kraken’s Unified Wallet documentation.
Collateral is credited at asset-specific ratios. For cross margin, the introductory documentation lists bitcoin and ether at 99% of their value and USD and EUR at 100%, with parameters subject to change.
Regional restrictions narrow the pool further. Kraken’s collateral valuation rules give USDT and DAI zero collateral value for EEA users through a 100% haircut.
Coin-M, or inverse, derivatives balances remain outside Unified Wallet. The support guide also keeps US TradFi futures separate.
Limiting a position’s exposure and switching back
For individual trades, isolated margin remains available on linear Multi-M futures contracts. It separates the margin allocated to a position, limiting that position’s potential trading losses to its allocation.
Users do not need to close open positions to enable Unified Wallet, but switching back to separate wallets requires closing all derivatives positions and active orders first.
After switching back, balances remain in Main. Users must manually transfer funds to the separate derivatives wallet before opening new positions there.

articles.title: Tom Lee’s Bitmine Adds $30 Million in Ethereum as Buying Nears Its Finish Line - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Bitmine bought another 12,535 ETH, raising its holdings to 6,041,481 ETH (about $14.3 billion), or 4.9% of supply—99% of the way to its “Alchemy of 5%” target.
- Chairman Tom Lee blamed recent crypto weakness on a broad risk-off shift—AI funding and safety fears, U.S.-Iran tensions, midterm jitters and rising bond yields—and called the dip a historically attractive risk-reward entry.
- Total holdings hit $15.1 billion, and Bitmine remains the top ETH treasury.
Bitmine Immersion Technologies kept its weekly Ethereum buying streak alive, adding 12,535 ETH worth about $30 million, even as a market-wide selloff battered crypto prices and the firm closed in on the end of its accumulation.
The NYSE-listed company said Monday its holdings now total 6,041,481 ETH, valued at roughly $14.3 billion at a reference price of $2,365 per coin. That represents 4.9% of Ethereum’s 122.1 million token supply, leaving Bitmine, by its own count, 99% of the way to its goal of owning 5% of the network, a target it calls the “Alchemy of 5%,” reached in just 15 months.
The purchase extends a run that hasn’t paused since Bitmine launched its treasury strategy on June 30, 2025, buying Ethereum every week since. Chairman Tom Lee has said the company is nearly finished stacking and will stop once it hits the 5% threshold. (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt’s parent company.)
This latest buy lands with the firm underwater on paper, a consequence of accumulating much of its stash last year at higher prices, with ETH now trading well below its highs.
Lee pinned the recent weakness on a broad contraction in risk appetite, citing anxiety over AI funding and model safety, escalating U.S.-Iran tensions, midterm-election jitters, and rising global bond yields.
He argued that selloffs in AI and semiconductor stocks in markets like Korea and Taiwan, where crypto is widely held, spilled over into digital assets, and framed the dip as a historically attractive risk-reward entry when fundamentals stay strong.
Counting cash, other tokens and what it calls “moonshot” investments, Bitmine’s total holdings reached $15.1 billion as of Oct. 18, including 215 Bitcoin, $582 million in cash and marketable securities, a $180 million stake in Beast Industries and a $74 million position in Eightco Holdings, which it bills as a rare public proxy for indirect OpenAI exposure.
Bitmine remains the world’s largest Ethereum treasury and the second-largest crypto treasury overall, trailing only Michael Saylor’s Strategy, which holds about 848,250 BTC.
Strategy recently added another $22 million in Bitcoin while buying back preferred stock. Bitmine has 5,067,309 ETH, about 84% of its holdings, staked through its MAVAN platform, with projected annualized revenue of roughly $309 million.

articles.title: Strategy Buys $22M in Bitcoin, Buys Back $193M of STRC - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Strategy bought 267 BTC for $22.1 million last week and repurchased $193.1 million of its STRC preferred stock, according to an SEC filing.
- Its board raised the cap on its digital credit securities repurchase program to $3 billion from $2 billion, leaving $1.16 billion available.
- The company funded the Bitcoin purchase mostly by selling MSTR common stock, while the STRC buybacks came from its cash reserves.
Strategy bought 267 BTC for $22.1 million last week and repurchased $193.1 million of its STRC preferred stock, the company said on Monday.
The Bitcoin treasury firm paid an average of $82,900 per coin, including fees, between October 12 and 18, according to an SEC filing. That compares with $86,194 a coin for the 250 BTC it bought the week before, Decrypt reported. Strategy now holds 848,517 BTC, acquired for a total of $64.02 billion at an average of $75,446 per coin.
Strategy has repurchased $193M of $STRC and acquired 267 $BTC. As of 10/18/26, we hold 848,517 BTC and $5.3B of USD Assets. We have also increased the size of our Digital Credit Securities Repurchase Program from $2.0B to $3.0B. $MSTRhttps://t.co/4o0bQBaTb0
— Strategy (@Strategy) October 19, 2026
The purchase is in line with last week's $21.5 million buy, and a fraction of the $142.7 million Strategy spent on Bitcoin in the last week of September.
Strategy co-founder Michael Saylor had hinted at the purchase in a tweet on Sunday, writing: "We found room for more orange."
Strategy paid for the purchase with $22 million raised by selling 140,872 shares of its MSTR common stock through its at-the-market offering program, plus $0.1 million of cash. It sold none of its preferred stock during the week.
The company bought back 1,938,780 shares of STRC, its variable-rate Stretch preferred stock, using $193.1 million of what it calls USD Cash, money set aside for general purposes including buying Bitcoin.
Strategy's board also raised the total authorized under its digital credit securities repurchase program, which covers its preferred stock, to $3 billion from $2 billion. Last week's buyback had left $354.8 million in the program; after this week's purchases and the increase, $1.16 billion remained available as of October 18. A separate program to buy back MSTR common stock has $1 billion left.
The company also used $45.5 million from its USD Reserve, which is meant to cover preferred dividends and interest on its debt, to pay dividends. As of October 18, the reserve held $4.83 billion and USD Cash $447.3 million, down from $4.88 billion and $640.5 million a week earlier.
Strategy and the MSCI rules
The repurchase extends a run of weekly STRC buybacks. Strategy bought back $192.4 million of the stock the previous week, and $176 million the week before that, as it bought $29 million in Bitcoin and posted a $21 billion third-quarter gain. In the last week of September, it repurchased $151.7 million of STRC as it took its holdings to a then-record 847,666 BTC.
The company is also facing possible removal from MSCI's widely tracked equity indexes. On October 15, the index provider finalized a rule that treats "non-operating companies," those whose balance sheets are dominated by a single asset, as ineligible for its Global Investable Market Indexes from the close of November 30. MSCI will publish the list of affected companies on November 11.
Removal would force funds that track the indexes to sell the affected shares. Saylor had urged MSCI to drop what he called a "discriminatory" rule.

articles.title: Strategy’s discretionary cash falls 72% as buyback authorization rises to $3 billion
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Strategy spent nearly nine times as much on STRC buybacks as Bitcoin last week and raised its preferred-stock repurchase authorization to $3 billion.
- Discretionary USD Cash fell to $447.3 million, alongside a separate $4.83 billion reserve intended for preferred dividends and debt interest.
- MSTR fell 11% amid MSCI exclusion concerns, testing bullish Wall Street forecasts and Strategy's ability to restart larger Bitcoin purchases.
Strategy's discretionary USD Cash fell to $447.3 million as the company spent another $193.1 million on STRC buybacks and raised its preferred-stock repurchase authorization to $3 billion.
The Michael Saylor-led company disclosed on Oct. 19 that it bought Bitcoin for $22.1 million at an average price of $82,900 over the previous week. The acquisitions increased its holdings to 848,517 BTC, accumulated for approximately $64.02 billion.
During the same period, Strategy spent another $193.1 million repurchasing nearly 1.94 million shares of its Variable Rate Series A Perpetual Stretch Preferred Stock (STRC), extending an aggressive campaign to support the security's trading price near its $100 stated value.
The firm's discretionary USD Cash holdings declined about 72% to $447.3 million as of Oct. 18, down from $1.61 billion on Aug. 30. The latest weekly decline of $193.2 million comprised $193.1 million in STRC repurchases and $100,000 in Bitcoin purchases.
Strategy financed $22 million of its latest Bitcoin acquisitions through the sale of 140,872 common shares, using just $100,000 of USD Cash for the remainder.
Meanwhile, its separate USD Reserve, designated primarily for dividend and debt-interest payments, stood at $4.83 billion after the company withdrew $45.5 million for preferred-stock dividends.
Strategy expands STRC buybacks despite spending $562 million near $99
Strategy's board increased its digital credit securities repurchase authorization by 50% to $3 billion from $2 billion, leaving approximately $1.16 billion available for additional purchases.
The expansion follows the company's spending roughly $1.84 billion to buy back STRC since it began repurchases in July.
Of that amount, the company deployed $713.5 million in the last four weeks through Oct. 18, including about $561.8 million during the three weeks beginning Sept. 28, when STRC traded between $99 and $100 for most of the period.
The sustained buying contrasts with Strategy's original plan to gradually reduce repurchases as the preferred stock approached its intended trading range.
In July, Chief Executive Officer Phong Le said the company would make larger purchases at deeper discounts and taper spending as STRC recovered toward par. Its initial purchases averaged about $86.53 per share, securing a discount of nearly 13.5%.
However, the latest repurchases averaged approximately $99.60 per share, a discount of just 0.4%. Strategy has continued deploying substantial capital, even as the immediate financial benefit of buying below stated value has narrowed.
Market commentator Mark Harvey observed that Strategy has repurchased about one-fifth of STRC's outstanding shares without securing a sustained return to $100. He questioned whether demand for the security was proving weaker than anticipated despite the scale of the company's intervention.
The continued expenditure also creates a funding challenge. As an illustration, the remaining $447.3 million in discretionary USD Cash would fund about 2.3 weeks of repurchases at the latest weekly pace of $193.1 million. Sustaining that pace would require replenishing USD Cash or using another funding source.
MSCI exclusion threat tests Wall Street's bullish Strategy outlook
Strategy's latest capital-management moves follow another difficult week for its common shareholders as index provider MSCI adopted new rules that could remove Bitcoin treasury companies from major global benchmarks.
MSTR fell 11.35% over the five trading sessions ended Oct. 16, declining from $154.34 to $136.83.
On Oct. 15, MSCI announced that companies classified as non-operating entities would become ineligible for its Global Investable Market Indexes. The changes potentially affect Strategy and Japan's Metaplanet, with the final list of affected companies scheduled for Nov. 11 ahead of implementation on Nov. 30.
The threat adds another pressure point on Strategy's equity financing model. A CoinDesk report shared by Ki Young Ju cited JPMorgan's estimate that exclusion from MSCI benchmarks could trigger approximately $2.8 billion in forced selling by passive investment funds.
VanEck's Matthew Sigel noted that STRC briefly reached $99.90 last week before falling to $97.72 following MSCI's announcement. He argued that preferred-stock indexes largely lack MSCI-linked ownership, making STRC's return to par a critical test of Strategy's ability to restart larger Bitcoin purchases through at-the-market offerings.
Nevertheless, CryptoQuant Consensus data shows that the analysts it tracks remain overwhelmingly bullish on Strategy despite the index-related uncertainty.
CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju pointed to price targets of $240 from Citigroup, $175 from Barclays and $195 from B. Riley, arguing that analyst expectations remain positive and that MSCI-related selling risks have largely been incorporated into MSTR's valuation.
Ju said the more consequential indicators were Strategy's market-value-to-net-asset-value ratio near one, STRC's proximity to par and the company's liquidity reserves supporting preferred dividends.
Strategy is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Oct. 29. MSCI will publish its final index deletion list on Nov. 11, ahead of the new rules taking effect after the Nov. 30 close.

articles.title: Bitcoin, Ether ETFs Shed $549M, October ETH Outflows Near $1B
articles.text:
Bitcoin, Ether ETFs shed $549M as October ETH outflows near $1B
US spot Ether ETFs recorded around $955 million in October net outflows so far, while Bitcoin funds extended their weekly withdrawal streak to two weeks.
US spot Bitcoin and Ether exchange-traded funds (ETFs) saw $549 million in net outflows last week as investors continued pulling money from two of the largest crypto funds.
Bitcoin ETFs recorded around $229 million in weekly net outflows, while Ether funds posted even higher withdrawals at $320 million, according to SoSoValue data.
The latest withdrawals marked a second consecutive week of losses for Bitcoin ETFs and a third for Ether funds. Outflows slowed from the previous week, when the two recorded $1.22 billion in net outflows.
Spot Ether ETFs have recorded roughly $955 million in net outflows so far in October, more than in any other month this year.
Ether (ETH) fell 5% over the past seven days to around $2,433, while Bitcoin dipped 1.3% to $82,783 at the time of publication, according to CoinGecko data.
Despite the withdrawals, both Bitcoin and Ether ETFs remain in positive territory for 2026, with Bitcoin ETFs attracting roughly $259 million in net inflows year-to-date and Ether ETFs drawing about $610 million.
Solana (SOL) ETFs recorded around $26 million in net withdrawals during the week, followed by Zcash (ZEC) at $19 million and Hyperliquid (HYPE) at $18 million, according to SoSoValue data. XRP and BNB funds saw smaller outflows of $1.8 million and $285,000, respectively.

articles.title: Morning Minute: Crypto Rebounds as 'Black Monday' Looms - Decrypt
articles.text:
Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.
GM!
Today’s top news:
- Crypto majors rebound despite Black Monday fears; BTC at $82k
- Bitcoin ETFs see $228M in net outflows this past week; ETH ETFs lost $320M
- Circle plans to expand into 40 emerging market countries
- Papertrade leads onchain protocols in revenue on week with $30M
- Trenches index hits “cold” for first time since April
📈 Crypto Rebounds as Black Monday Looms
Thirty-nine years ago today, the Dow fell 22.6% in a single session. Nobody saw it coming, and the notorious “Black Monday” turned into trading history.
Crypto enters that anniversary bruised but not broken. Bitcoin sits at $82,161, down just 1.4% on the week and actually up about 1% over the last 30 days. That’s the good news and it’s nearly the only good news.
Everything else got hit harder. Ethereum fell 5.3% to $2,415. BNB dropped 3.3%, Solana 6.2%, XRP 7.2%, Dogecoin 9.4%, Hyperliquid 8.6%, Zcash 13.2%. Across the majors, the average decline outside Bitcoin was 7.5%—roughly five times what BTC gave up.
Further out it gets ugly. Starknet lost 45% on the week, LayerZero 24%, Pump.fun 22%, Ethena 20%, Fetch 20%, Midnight 19%, Canton 18%, Jupiter 18%, Filecoin 17%, Raydium 18%. The top twelve weekly losers averaged losses of more than 20%. And all of this happened in just seven days.
The ETFs bled out as well. Spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $228.4 million across the week, Ethereum ETFs $320.1 million, for a combined $548.5 million. For October, the two complexes have now bled $1.86 billion. Ethereum’s situation is the more fragile one: $14.5 billion in net assets against $12.9 billion of cumulative inflows leaves barely $1.6 billion of cushion before the entire product line is underwater on a mark-to-market basis.
But for context, what turned a bad Friday into Black Monday back then was automated selling feeding automated selling, with no circuit breakers to interrupt it. Equities have those now, and Korea’s Kospi actually tripped one last week. Crypto has none. It trades through the weekend, through the open, through everything, and we already watched what that looks like on October 10, 2025 when the liquidation cascade repriced the whole market in hours.
The setup today is the opposite of a cascade. Slow bleed, orderly exits, Bitcoin holding while the tail gets cut off—and over the weekend, a modest bid returning across the board. And there is broad concern for a “Black Monday” occurring today. Which very likely in itself means it won’t happen. Crashes don’t occur when everyone is expecting them and ready with cash on the sidelines.
The bears may want a Black Monday, but they are very unlikely to get it. At least today…
🌎 Macro Crypto and Markets
- Crypto majors are flat on the day but rebounding from a Sunday selloff; BTC even at $82.4k; ETH even at $2,422; SOL +1% at $105; HYPE even at $79; ZEC +1% at $1,146
- Top alt movers include RAY (+8%), ARB (+8%), VVV (+6%) and PEPE (+6%)
- Oil +4% at $101; Gold +0.4% at $4,200
- Stock futures are green after news of a Putin peace summit incoming; DOW -0.1%, Nasdaq +1.1%
- Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley all told third-quarter earnings calls that tokenization is a growth opportunity rather than a threat, with David Solomon comparing it to the shift to electronic stock trading and Wells Fargo revealing its tokenized-deposit payments system is already in production

articles.title: Wall Street's Bitcoin bears quietly retreated despite recent plunge toward $80,000
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Hedge funds cut net bearish Bitcoin futures positions by nearly 15%, reducing short exposure by 5,292 BTC as prices tumbled toward $80,000.
- The shift came as Bitcoin ETFs recorded nearly $230 million in weekly outflows, while leveraged traders increased spread positions by 48%.
- Bitcoin's subsequent slide below $80,000 raises questions about whether hedge funds continued unwinding shorts or rebuilt bearish positions.
Hedge funds cut their net bearish Bitcoin futures bets nearly 15% even as the cryptocurrency tumbled toward $80,000.
Data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) showed leveraged funds held a net short position equivalent to 30,611 BTC as of Oct. 13, down from 35,903 BTC a week earlier.
The 5,292 BTC reduction came as Bitcoin fell nearly 3% during the reporting period, from about $85,600 on Oct. 6 to $83,100 on Oct. 13. The cryptocurrency briefly slipped below $81,000 as rising Treasury yields, weakening institutional demand, and a global technology stock selloff weighed on risk appetite.
The decline gave bearish traders opportunities to take profits, while repeated price reversals increased the risk of holding leveraged positions.
CFTC figures showed that outright short positions declined by 6,437 BTC to 59,458 BTC, compared with a smaller reduction of 1,145 BTC in outright longs to 28,847 BTC.
The faster decline in shorts narrowed the bearish imbalance, although leveraged funds maintained more than twice as much outright short exposure as long exposure.
Bitcoin's decline exposes traders to mounting market pressure
Bitcoin's weakness accelerated on Oct. 7 as Treasury yields approached 5.3% and expectations of additional Federal Reserve tightening weighed on speculative assets.
Elevated oil prices reinforced concerns about persistent inflation, while higher bond yields increased the relative appeal of interest-bearing investments.
The cryptocurrency subsequently fell below $81,000 on Oct. 8, extending a retreat from levels near $87,000 earlier in the month. The decline weakened confidence in Bitcoin's late-September recovery, particularly as demand through US-listed exchange-traded funds deteriorated.
Market volatility intensified again on Oct. 13 as a sharp selloff in South Korean semiconductor stocks spread through Asian equities.
As CryptoSlate reported, South Korea's KOSPI plunged about 5.5%, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix suffering heavy losses amid concerns about the financing and profitability of artificial intelligence investments.
The selloff coincided with approximately $813 million in cryptocurrency liquidations over 24 hours, including $686.72 million in bullish positions. Bitcoin briefly fell below $81,000 before rebounding above $83,000.
The resulting price swings made large directional positions increasingly risky, giving leveraged funds an economic incentive to reduce exposure even as Bitcoin remained under pressure.
Hedge funds increase spread positions by 48% as futures exposure contracts
While leveraged funds reduced outright bearish exposure, they increased positions involving offsetting long and short Bitcoin futures contracts.
CFTC data showed spreading positions rose by 2,719 BTC-equivalent per leg to about 8,434 BTC, up nearly 48% during the reporting week.
Such strategies can involve buying futures contracts with one expiration date while selling contracts expiring in another month, allowing traders to seek returns from differences in futures pricing while limiting directional exposure.
The increase lifted gross long exposure by 1,574 BTC to approximately 37,281 BTC, even though outright bullish positions declined.
Gross short exposure, meanwhile, fell by 3,718 BTC to 67,891 BTC as increased spreading activity partly offset the reduction in directional shorts.
The change coincided with a broader contraction in participation in CME Bitcoin futures. Combined open interest across standard and micro Bitcoin contracts declined by approximately 3,567 BTC-equivalent, or 3.2%, during the week.
Together, the figures show leveraged funds reducing outright market exposure while committing more capital to offsetting futures positions.
Asset managers maintained a contrasting profile, holding approximately 18,440 BTC-equivalent in net long positions. Their bullish imbalance rose by roughly 547 BTC, mainly because short holdings fell faster than long positions.
However, Bitcoin's subsequent performance complicated the outlook for both groups.
On Oct. 14, hotter-than-expected US consumer inflation revived expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase, sending Bitcoin below $83,000.
The following day, a sharp increase in wholesale inflation pushed the cryptocurrency to approximately $79,730 and triggered $939 million in cryptocurrency liquidations.
Bitcoin later recovered to about $82,800 on Oct. 19, though the market remained vulnerable to further selling. CryptoSlate reported that Glassnode identified a significant concentration of buying interest near $80,000, with the next major support around $78,000 if that level fails.
Those movements occurred after the latest CFTC positioning snapshot, raising questions about whether leveraged funds continued reducing bearish exposure or rebuilt short positions during the renewed selloff.
The next CFTC report, scheduled for Oct. 23 and covering positions as of Oct. 20, will offer the first indication of how hedge funds responded to Bitcoin's latest inflation-driven decline and whether the earlier reduction in bearish bets continued as the cryptocurrency struggled to establish support above $80,000.

articles.title: Zoom Adds ‘Proof of Human’ Badges to Fight AI Deepfakes
articles.text:
Zoom adds ‘proof of human’ badges to show you’re not a deepfake
Sam Altman-backed World has rolled out biometric verification badges for Zoom enterprise users, aiming to combat AI deepfake impersonation and fraud.
Zoom enterprise customers will now be able to see “proof of human” badges to verify that people appearing on video calls are real, after a global rollout of biometric identity technology from World.
On Sunday, the Sam Altman-backed project announced that World ID for Zoom is now available in the Zoom Marketplace. The system compares an image captured by the company’s iris-scanning Orb, a live selfie and the participant’s video feed before displaying a Human Badge visible to other meeting participants.
World first announced its Zoom integration in April, when it was undergoing limited beta testing with VanEck Funds. The feature is now available globally to Zoom enterprise customers. World also named Bain Capital, Pantera Capital and other financial firms as initial design partners for its broader identity verification technology.
The rollout follows incidents involving AI-generated impersonation. In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup transferred about $25 million after scammers impersonated executives during a video conference.
In February, suspected North Korea-linked hackers used fabricated video feeds in fake Zoom meetings to trick crypto and fintech companies into installing malware.
“World ID for Zoom is designed to protect sensitive, high-stakes conversations by proving that a real and unique human is present,” World said in a statement cited by Fortune.
Related: New AI cybercrime tool targets crypto, bank KYC systems via deepfakes

articles.title: South Korea Faces Calls to Delay Crypto Tax to 2029
articles.text:
South Korea to meet crypto exchanges amid calls for tax delay
Finance officials are reportedly set to meet major crypto exchanges on Tuesday, days after a lawmaker introduced legislation that could push the tax’s start date back two years.
South Korea’s senior finance officials are reportedly set to meet crypto exchanges on Tuesday as calls to postpone a planned cryptocurrency tax are heating up ahead of its scheduled implementation in January.
According to Yonhap, the government is planning to hold a consultation on crypto taxation, with representatives coming from Upbit, Bithumb, Coinone, DigitalX and Gopax, along with executives of the Digital Asset Exchange Alliance, known as DAXA.
Government officials attending include Kwon Dae-young, first vice minister of finance and economy, and Yoo Young-jun, director general for digital financial policy at the Financial Services Commission.
South Korean regulators have delayed the crypto tax three times, with the latest delay pushing the start date to 2027 amid political disagreement and industry pushback over exchange readiness and the threshold level.
An exchange official told Yonhap on Sunday that unresolved transaction rules and limited time to prepare infrastructure supported postponing the tax.
“Standards for different transaction types have not yet been finalized, and time is running short for practical preparations on the infrastructure side,” an exchange official told Yonhap. “There is a shared view in favor of postponing the start of taxation.”
On Friday, Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Park Min-gyu introduced a bill seeking to postpone the tax until Jan. 1 of the second year after South Korea begins sharing data under OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). With the first exchange expected in 2027, taxation would begin in 2029.
Related: South Korea plans cybersecurity overhaul after attacks hit banks, crypto firms

articles.title: ‘Terrifying Precedent’: Dutch Hand US Data From Seized Anti-Fascist Server - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Police in Amsterdam, Netherlands seized a server belonging to an anti-fascist group Autistici/Inventati (A/I), following a request from U.S. authorities.
- The U.S. designated the group as a "Specially Designated Global Terrorist" in August, claiming that it offered digital infrastructure to "far-left militants."
- A privacy advocate slams the politically motivated seizure as a "terrifying precedent," while a legal expert questions if the Dutch considered their legal right to refuse.
A Dutch-based server belonging to an anti-fascist political group was seized by police in Amsterdam last week. It followed a request from U.S. authorities, the NL Times reported Saturday, after the Trump administration designated the group as a "global terrorist" organization.
The seized server belonged to Italian internet service provider Autistici/Inventati (A/I), an anti-capitalist and anti-fascist group which offered free email and web-hosting services for organizations and activists. Police seized the server from a data center in Amsterdam's eastern district, and Dutch authorities are now handing its data over to the U.S.
Privacy advocate Harry Halpin told Decrypt that "politically motivated server seizures" set a "terrifying precedent." And one legal expert questioned whether the Dutch considered their legal right to refuse.
Halpin, CEO of privacy infrastructure firm Nym, told Decrypt, argued that the targeting of Autistici/Inventati servers by the Trump administration was "due to their political beliefs," adding that, "The fact that the Dutch authorities co-operated with them to shut down a server means that the Netherlands is nothing more than a colony of the United States."
The U.S. designated Autistici/Inventati as a "Specially Designated Global Terrorist" in August, claiming that it operates the "digital infrastructure for violent Antifa cells and other far-left militants."
The designation prevents U.S.-based people and organizations from doing business with them. In turn, Autistici/Inventati disbanded as its users and donors faced potential repercussions.
One legal expert said the designation has no standing in the Netherlands and that another legal power was exercised.
"An FBI agent in Amsterdam has roughly the powers of a tourist," Yuriy Brisov, lawyer and partner at Digital & Analogue Partners, told Decrypt. "So states ask each other permission. For the United States and the EU states, the rulebook for asking is a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty, or MLAT, signed in The Hague in 1981."
Brisov explained that everything is done "under Dutch law, by Dutch officers, with Dutch powers," but entirely at the request of the U.S. For that reason, he said, Dutch authorities seized the server and not the U.S.
Prosecutors operate on a “trust principle,” the legal expert told Decrypt, meaning they don’t assess whether the seizure is proportionate or whether the U.S. investigation actually needs the material.
However, Brisov said, the Dutch could choose to refuse the request if it "harms its essential interests, concerns a political offence, or amounts to double jeopardy." Seizure is also only allowed if the alleged conduct is a crime in both countries carrying more than a year in prison.
It is important to note that designating a group as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist doesn't require a conviction or a court to hear the case, Brisov added, and neither the Dutch government nor the European Union followed the U.S. designation.
"Here is the Dutch problem: Washington's label underpins the request, and the Netherlands does not share it," Brisov told Decrypt, questioning whether "anyone in The Hague asked the political-offence question" that Dutch law reserves for Minister of Justice and Security David van Weel personally. "Internet hosts are not normally liable for what their users do," Brisov noted, adding that the rule is written into both U.S. law and EU law through the Digital Services Act.
Halpin told Decrypt that the request should have been scrutinized due to its political nature.
"Any country that believes in sovereignty should push back against politically motivated server seizures," he said. "This shows that only a multi-jurisdictional setup with true decentralization, as attempted by many blockchain projects, is the only way to resist nation-state-level attacks on digital infrastructure."

articles.title: Tether loses nearly $5 billion across crypto exchanges as USDC and RLUSD rivals pay to win liquidity
articles.text:
Quick Take
- USDT balances fell $4.6 billion across 19 selected exchanges and lenders in Q3, while those institutions added $1.9 billion in competing stablecoins.
- USDC and RLUSD gained ground as exchanges embraced rewards and revenue-sharing deals, intensifying competition for billions in cryptocurrency trading.
- Tether still controlled 84% of stablecoin payments, raising questions about whether exchange incentives can eventually erode its market dominance.
Tether lost $4.6 billion in USDT supply across 19 selected cryptocurrency exchanges and lenders during the third quarter as rival stablecoins gained ground.
During the same period, the 19 institutions added approximately $1.9 billion in competing tokens, including $569 million of Circle's USDC and $493 million of Ripple's RLUSD.
According to the Crystal Intelligence report, Bybit recorded the largest reduction, shedding $1.66 billion in USDT while adding $315 million of RLUSD. Binance reduced its Tether holdings by $987 million and acquired $223 million of USDC, while OKX cut $899 million in USDT and added $273 million of USDC.
Across the wider market, USDT's circulating supply fell $647 million, or 0.4%, to about $184 billion during the quarter. Meanwhile, RLUSD rose 59% to $2.5 billion, while USDC gained $687 million.
The changes reflect growing competition for cryptocurrency trading balances, as issuers and their distribution partners offer financial incentives to exchanges and customers who hold their tokens.
Crypto exchanges increasingly profit from stablecoin holdings
The competition has become especially visible in cryptocurrency derivatives markets, where stablecoins serve as trading collateral and can generate additional income for platforms that hold customer deposits.
Hyperliquid, a leading derivative trading platform, recorded a $1.5 billion increase in USDC deposits during the quarter, bringing its holdings to approximately $7.2 billion.
The growth coincided with an arrangement between Coinbase and Circle that lets Hyperliquid receive income from USDC deployed on the platform.
Under Hyperliquid's Aligned Quote Assets framework, Coinbase serves as USDC's treasury deployer, while Circle manages the technical infrastructure. Coinbase shares most of the reserve-linked income with Hyperliquid, with the arrangement specifying payments based on a cost-adjusted reference rate.
That provides Hyperliquid with revenue tied to the collateral supporting its derivatives business. Crystal found that approximately three-quarters of the platform's quarterly USDC increase came from one cluster of linked wallets.
Deribit, the largest derivatives trading exchange, has adopted a different strategy, rewarding customers directly for maintaining USDC balances. The Coinbase-owned platform added $365 million in USDC during the quarter and expanded its rewards program to approximately 70 additional countries in August.
Under the program, qualifying customers receive monthly payments calculated using their daily minimum USDC holdings.
Other issuers are pursuing similar arrangements. Bybit's RLUSD holdings increased following a rewards campaign launched with Ripple in July, while Bitget and MEXC accumulated USDGO through holding incentives and conversion promotions.
The competition extends into decentralized lending. Spark placed about $247 million in RLUSD into a Morpho vault run by Sentora, accounting for most of Morpho's $404 million quarterly increase across six stablecoins.
These commercial agreements are becoming increasingly expensive for issuers seeking access to exchanges, lending platforms and their customers.
Circle's own financial results illustrate the rising cost of competing for stablecoin distribution. The company generated about $1.4 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026 but spent $819 million, or 59% of that amount, on distribution and transaction costs.
Another $473 million went to operating expenses and network investment, leaving Circle with about $103 million in net profit, or just seven cents of every revenue dollar.
Coinbase remains Circle's largest distribution partner, with average USDC holdings across its products reaching a record $20 billion in the second quarter, up 44% from a year earlier. Circle has since expanded its distribution network through a five-year agreement with Binance, which also invested $100 million in the stablecoin issuer.
Other issuers are adopting comparable revenue-sharing models to secure distribution.
PayPal-backed PYUSD supports a program offering a 4.5% incentive on up to $1 billion in deposits through USD.AI, while Stripe-owned Bridge launched Open USD in September with a model designed to return most reserve income to distribution partners.
These arrangements give exchanges and financial applications greater bargaining power when deciding which stablecoins to support. Issuers seeking additional circulation face competing demands for a larger share of the income generated by their reserves.
Tether retains dominance in $482 billion stablecoin payments market
Despite shifting trading balances, USDT maintained a commanding position in stablecoin payments during the first nine months of 2026.
A separate report from Allium estimated that stablecoins processed $482 billion in classified payments between January and September, with USDT accounting for 84% of the total.
That represents approximately $405 billion in USDT payment value, compared with $77 billion across competing stablecoins. This shows Tether's continued importance in commercial transactions, even as rival issuers expand on derivatives platforms and in decentralized lending markets.
USDT also maintained significant liquidity on centralized exchanges. Crystal estimated that named exchanges held approximately $85 billion in tracked stablecoins at the end of September, with Tether representing roughly two-thirds of those holdings. Binance alone held $41 billion of USDT.
Meanwhile, the broader stablecoin payments market continued expanding faster than circulating supply.
Allium reported that payment value increased 45% from the corresponding period last year, while transaction counts climbed 71% to 1.04 billion.
The average payment declined from $544 to $462, reflecting more small, frequent transactions. September recorded $72 billion in payments, the highest monthly total in Allium's dataset.
The Tron blockchain processed approximately two-thirds of classified payment value, preserving a major distribution network for USDT as stablecoins gained traction in business and consumer transfers.
That established payments footprint further challenges issuers seeking to expand beyond trading collateral. Winning exchange deposits through financial incentives gives competitors access to liquidity, while expanding payment usage requires adoption by wallets, merchants and businesses moving money.

articles.title: Qubic Halts Blockchain After $1.4M Wallet Theft
articles.text:
Qubic freezes chain after attacker drains 1.4K wallets with weak seeds
Qubic says 87.1% of the stolen funds remain onchain and the rest were frozen at crypto exchange MEXC, as network validators prepare to vote on a recovery plan.
Layer-1 blockchain network Qubic halted operations Sunday after an attacker reportedly exploited weakly generated wallet seeds to drain approximately $1.4 million from more than 1,400 accounts, according to the project.
In a statement on X, Qubic said the network was halted at tick 85,371,949, where it remains paused at the time of writing. Qubic said the vulnerability affected wallet seeds generated using any browser on an iPhone or iPad, Safari on a Mac until Oct. 18, 2026, or the Qubic iOS app before July 2025, leading to 2.94 trillion Qubit (QU) stolen.
“87.1% of the drained funds never left the Qubic network and remain frozen in place,” said Qubic. “The remaining 12.9% was sent to MEXC, whose team froze the receiving account within about an hour.”
The Qubic theft is the latest in a series of attacks tied to weak wallet seeds. In July, Coldcard disclosed that attackers had stolen funds from wallets whose seeds were weakened by a firmware bug. Similar flaws affected Trust Wallet’s browser extension and the Libbitcoin Explorer tool in 2023.
Related: Bitget’s $388M hack pushes Q3 crypto security losses past $1B
Qubic said it has fixed the seed-generation flaw in the latest version of its web wallet.
A GitHub commit for version 4.26.4 shows that Qubic replaced JavaScript’s Math.random() function, which is not suitable for generating cryptographic secrets, with the cryptographically secure crypto.getRandomValues() function when creating wallet seeds.
Qubic said its core team is identifying affected wallets and preparing recovery options for a vote by the network’s Computors, which will decide what happens to the frozen funds. The team said it would publish a full technical report after a recovery plan is settled. It has not announced when the network will restart.
Qubic did not immediately respond to Cointelegraph’s request for comment.
Qubic is a layer-1 blockchain that supports transactions and smart contracts without fees. It is built on Useful Proof of Work (UPoW) – a consensus mechanism that repurposes mining energy to train artificial intelligence. Qubic’s token had a market capitalization of about $62.6 million at the time of writing, according to CoinGecko.
In the third quarter, hacks and exploits accounted for 19% of crypto crime cases but 40% of reported losses, according to AMLBot’s 2026 investigations report, which looked at 250 investigations it opened since the start of the year.
Magazine: Richard Heart caught ‘off-guard,’ QDay gets even closer: Hodler’s Digest

articles.title: Sam Altman's World Takes Proof-of-Human IDs to Banks, Citing $40B AI Fraud Risk - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- World, the identity project co-founded by Sam Altman, has launched World ID for banking and finance to help institutions confirm that real humans are behind transactions.
- Bain Capital, Pantera Capital, VanEck Funds, OpenExchange and Outtake are design partners, World said, pointing to forecasts of rising AI-enabled fraud.
- The project's iris-scanning Orbs have drawn regulatory action in countries including Spain, Kenya, Brazil and Hong Kong over biometric data concerns.
World co-founder Alex Blania has unveiled World ID for banking and finance, a suite of tools that lets financial institutions confirm a real person is behind transactions, trades and customer requests, the company said on Sunday.
Bain Capital, OpenExchange, Outtake, Pantera Capital and VanEck Funds are initial design partners, according to World.
The offering is built on three cryptographic proofs available through the World ID app. Proof of Human establishes that someone is a real and unique person through a one-time visit to one of World's Orb devices. Proof of Presence uses a selfie liveness check on a phone, while Proof of Attributes confirms details such as nationality or age from a government ID, revealing only the requested information.
Banks could use the proofs to require a verified human to approve ACH and wire transfers, or to recover an account, without collecting documents or storing other personal data, World said. AgentKit, a developer toolkit still in beta, lets users delegate certain proofs to AI agents so they can transact on a person's behalf.
The suite also includes World ID for Zoom, which builds on the project's earlier integrations with Zoom and Tinder. Participants verified at one of the project’s Orb devices get a "Human Badge" on their video tile after a live selfie check, and hosts will soon be able to require verification in the waiting room before a call.
World pointed to the case of an employee at engineering firm Arup who wired about $25.6 million in early 2024 after a video call in which every other participant was a deepfake. Deloitte forecasts that AI-enabled fraud losses in the U.S. could reach $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023, the company noted.
More than 18 million people hold a Proof of Human ID, according to World, with the World Foundation raising $52.5 million this year to scale the network.
In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup transferred $25.6 million after joining a video call where every other participant was a deepfake. Since then, AI has advanced significantly and is making impersonation increasingly convincing, causing challenges for financial… pic.twitter.com/J06gnULw8H
— World (@worldnetwork) October 19, 2026
World and privacy regulators
World's iris-scanning model has faced pushback from regulators around the world over its handling of biometric data.
Hong Kong's privacy watchdog ordered the project to stop its iris-scanning operations in 2024, while later that year South Korea's privacy regulator fined the project $830,000. That December, Spain's data protection agency told it to delete all iris scan data.
Last year, a Kenyan court ordered it to delete biometric user data, and Brazil's data protection authority denied its appeal against a ban.
