articles.title: What's the point of the 2.5G Ethernet port on your router? - Engadget
articles.text:
What's the point of the 2.5G Ethernet port on your router?
Faster speeds are great, but diminishing returns start to creep in.
Having fast internet at home involves more than just the plan you get from your ISP; you should understand what options your router provides to get the best possible performance. Part of that is knowing which Ethernet ports to use on your router, with one of the available choices potentially being 2.5G Ethernet.
A standard Ethernet port, which may be marked as LAN or have no label, typically maxes out at a speed of 1 Gbps. Meanwhile, a 2.5G port can provide speeds of up to 2.5 Gbps. These will be marked accordingly on your router, with a label in the vein of 2.5G or 2.5GbE. Ports capable of those zippier speeds might also use a different color than the basic ones.
When to use the 2.5G Ethernet port
There are a couple of requirements for being able to take advantage of a 2.5 Gbps port. In addition to your router needing this, your computer or other connected device must also have a 2.5 Gbps port. You'll also need a compatible Ethernet cable; Cat5e and anything newer are all equipped to deliver 2.5Gbps speeds. Anything limited to an older standard will become a bottleneck.
To fully take advantage of the faster speed in most practical uses, your internet plan also needs to be at least 2.5 Gbps. Otherwise, downloading and uploading data from the internet will be capped at the level of your ISP plan. However, even with slower internet, you can still take advantage of the faster speeds with devices on your local network. For example, backing up files to a NAS can run at the full 2.5 Gbps if all devices are compatible.
Otherwise, the main benefit of 2.5Gbps is obviously the increased speed. With a connection that's 2.5 times faster than what standard Ethernet ports offer, expect quick loading and downloading times when using that connection. For most people, multi-gig internet speeds are a nice-to-have rather than a must-have, with diminishing returns above 1 Gbps. But if you regularly perform tasks that tax your bandwidth, more than doubling your speed on those devices could make a difference.
It's a big help when conducting large file transfers or cloud backups, but it's not going to make Netflix run any smoother or improve your online game performance unless the rest of your network is extremely busy. Those activities don't require much bandwidth to begin with.

articles.title: Ngân hàng rao bán cả lô 5 xe ô tô Mitsubishi giá khởi điểm chỉ như 1 xe mới
articles.text:
Ngân hàng TMCP Đại chúng Việt Nam (PVcomBank) vừa thông báo đấu giá tài sản thông qua Công ty Đấu giá Hợp danh Minh Pháp. Tài sản đấu giá là nguyên lô 5 chiếc xe ô tô Mitsubishi Attrage. Giấy chứng nhận đăng ký của cả 5 xe đều do Phòng Cảnh sát giao thông Công an TPHCM cấp ngày 7/8/2019
PVcomBank cho biết chỉ bán nguyên lô cả 5 chiếc, không bán tách rời.
Giá khởi điểm của lô xe này là 371,78 triệu đồng, bình quân khoảng 74,36 triệu đồng/chiếc. Mức giá trên chưa bao gồm các khoản thuế, phí và lệ phí.
5 chiếc xe ô tô con 5 chỗ nhãn hiệu Mitsubishi Attrage đều có màu xám, lần lượt mang biển kiểm soát: 51H-115.67, 51H-117.76, 51H-115.27, 51H-116.86, 51H-119.01.
Ngân hàng bàn giao hồ sơ pháp lý và xe theo hiện trạng thực tế; người trúng đấu giá tự thực hiện thủ tục sang tên và các thủ tục liên quan.
Người tham gia đấu giá phải nộp tiền đặt trước bằng 20% giá khởi điểm, tương đương 74,356 triệu đồng.
Thời gian xem tài sản từ 8h ngày 16/10 đến 17h ngày 21/10 tại bãi xe 4S Linh Đông, 17/6i đường 22, phường Hiệp Bình, TPHCM.
Xe này hiện có giá khoảng 380 triệu đồng/chiếc với xe số sàn, trên 400 triệu đồng/chiếc với xe số tự động, chưa gồm thuế phí để lăn bánh.

articles.title: 5 chiếc iPhone giảm giá sâu, đáng mua nhất hiện nay
articles.text:
Năm chiếc iPhone này được bán với mức giá tốt hơn trong tháng 10, mang tới cơ hội mua máy với chi phí tiết kiệm hơn.
Sau khi thế hệ iPhone Duo xuất hiện, giá bán của một số mẫu iPhone đời trước lại được điều chỉnh tại các hệ thống bán lẻ. Đây là cơ hội để người dùng nâng cấp thiết bị với chi phí thấp hơn.
Trong tháng 10, 5 mẫu máy đáng chú ý gồm iPhone Air, iPhone 16, iPhone 13, iPhone 17 Pro Max và iPhone 17. Mỗi sản phẩm hướng đến một nhóm nhu cầu khác nhau, từ ưu tiên thiết kế, tiết kiệm chi phí đến yêu cầu cao về hiệu năng và camera.
1. iPhone Air
Trong số các mẫu máy được đề cập, iPhone Air ghi nhận mức giảm giá lớn nhất, lên tới 13 triệu đồng. Sản phẩm hướng đến người dùng ưu tiên thiết kế mỏng nhẹ, thay vì hệ thống camera đa dụng hay thời lượng pin thuộc nhóm cao nhất.
Máy có độ dày 5,6 mm, trọng lượng 165 g và màn hình 6,5 inch. Thiết kế này phù hợp với người thường xuyên mang điện thoại theo bên mình, sử dụng thiết bị trong thời gian dài hoặc đề cao tính gọn nhẹ.
Tuy nhiên, thiết kế mỏng cũng đặt ra những đánh đổi mà người mua cần cân nhắc, đặc biệt về thời lượng pin và khả năng chụp ảnh so với các mẫu iPhone có hệ thống camera phong phú hơn. Vì vậy, mức giảm sâu chưa phải yếu tố duy nhất quyết định giá trị của sản phẩm.
Với giá khởi điểm 23,39 triệu đồng theo thông tin bán lẻ được cung cấp, iPhone Air có thể cạnh tranh với iPhone 17 ở một số phiên bản và cửa hàng. Người mua nên đối chiếu dung lượng lưu trữ, chính sách bảo hành và nhu cầu sử dụng thực tế trước khi lựa chọn.
2. iPhone 16
iPhone 16 là phương án đáng cân nhắc với người muốn nâng cấp từ những thế hệ cũ nhưng chưa có nhu cầu sở hữu dòng máy cao cấp mới nhất. Trong tháng 10/2026, sản phẩm được ghi nhận mức giảm tối đa 5,8 triệu đồng, dù nguồn hàng và lựa chọn màu sắc có thể khác nhau giữa các đại lý.
Máy sử dụng chip A18, màn hình Super Retina XDR 6,1 inch, camera chính 48 MP và camera góc siêu rộng 12 MP. Nút Action, Camera Control cùng cổng USB-C giúp mở rộng khả năng thao tác và tăng tính thuận tiện khi sử dụng phụ kiện.
iPhone 16 cũng hỗ trợ Apple Intelligence trên các thiết bị, ngôn ngữ và khu vực đáp ứng yêu cầu của Apple. Đây là một trong những điểm đáng chú ý khi so sánh với các mẫu iPhone đời thấp hơn.
Với người đang sử dụng iPhone 12 hoặc iPhone 13, việc chuyển sang iPhone 16 có thể mang lại cải thiện về hiệu năng, camera và các tính năng phần mềm. Tuy nhiên, nếu giá iPhone 17 không chênh lệch nhiều tại thời điểm mua, người dùng nên so sánh cả hai thế hệ trước khi quyết định.
3. iPhone 13
iPhone 13 là mẫu máy có mức giá thấp nhất trong danh sách, phù hợp với người dùng muốn tiết kiệm chi phí hoặc không cần những tính năng mới nhất. Tuy nhiên, do sản phẩm đã ra mắt từ năm 2021, tình trạng hàng hóa cần được kiểm tra kỹ.
Máy được trang bị màn hình OLED 6,1 inch, chip A15 Bionic, hệ thống camera kép 12 MP và khả năng quay video 4K. Cấu hình này vẫn đáp ứng các nhu cầu phổ biến như liên lạc, sử dụng mạng xã hội, xem video và chụp ảnh hằng ngày.
Lợi thế của iPhone 13 nằm ở thiết kế nhỏ gọn và khả năng đáp ứng những tác vụ cơ bản. Dù vậy, tuổi đời thiết bị khiến thời gian hỗ trợ phần mềm còn lại trở thành yếu tố quan trọng khi cân nhắc mua máy.
Người mua cũng cần phân biệt hàng mới tồn kho với máy đã qua sử dụng hoặc hàng tân trang, đồng thời kiểm tra tình trạng pin, linh kiện và chính sách bảo hành. Với mức giá từ 14,29 triệu đồng theo thông tin được cung cấp, iPhone 13 chỉ thực sự hấp dẫn khi tình trạng máy và chế độ hậu mãi tương xứng với số tiền bỏ ra.
4. iPhone 17 Pro Max
Ở phân khúc cao cấp, iPhone 17 Pro Max là lựa chọn dành cho người cần màn hình lớn, hiệu năng mạnh và hệ thống camera linh hoạt. Sau khi thế hệ iPhone 18 Pro và iPhone 18 Pro Max xuất hiện, một số đại lý điều chỉnh giá bán iPhone 17 Pro Max, với mức giảm được ghi nhận lên tới 3 triệu đồng.
Sản phẩm có màn hình 6,9 inch, phù hợp với nhu cầu xem video, chơi game, đọc tài liệu và xử lý công việc trên điện thoại. Hệ thống camera cùng cấu hình cao cấp cũng hướng đến người thường xuyên chụp ảnh, quay video hoặc sử dụng các ứng dụng đòi hỏi nhiều tài nguyên.
So với việc mua thế hệ mới nhất, lựa chọn iPhone 17 Pro Max có thể giúp người dùng tiết kiệm một khoản chi phí mà vẫn tiếp cận được nhiều tính năng cao cấp. Dù vậy, mức giá khởi điểm 34,99 triệu đồng vẫn thuộc nhóm cao trên thị trường.
Với người chủ yếu nhắn tin, lướt web, xem video và chụp ảnh thông thường, những mẫu iPhone có giá thấp hơn có thể đáp ứng tốt nhu cầu. Ngược lại, người thường xuyên quay dựng video, chơi game hoặc khai thác hệ thống camera sẽ có thêm lý do để cân nhắc dòng Pro Max.
5. iPhone 17
iPhone 17 là phương án trung hòa giữa chi phí và khả năng sử dụng đối với người muốn sở hữu phần cứng thế hệ mới mà không cần đầu tư cho dòng Pro Max. Theo mức giá được cung cấp, sản phẩm hiện có giá từ 26,99 triệu đồng, với mức giảm tối đa 3 triệu đồng tại một số hệ thống bán lẻ.
Máy sở hữu màn hình 6,3 inch hỗ trợ ProMotion 120 Hz, chip A19 và hệ thống camera sau gồm camera chính 48 MP cùng camera góc siêu rộng 48 MP. Tần số quét cao giúp thao tác cuộn trang và các chuyển động trên màn hình mượt mà hơn.
So với iPhone Air, iPhone 17 hướng đến trải nghiệm sử dụng cân bằng hơn, không đặt trọng tâm quá lớn vào độ mỏng. Trong khi đó, so với iPhone 17 Pro Max, phiên bản tiêu chuẩn có mức giá dễ tiếp cận hơn nhưng không nhắm đến cùng nhóm nhu cầu chuyên sâu.
Đối với người đang sử dụng iPhone đời cũ, iPhone 17 có thể là lựa chọn phù hợp nếu muốn nâng cấp màn hình, hiệu năng và camera. Tuy nhiên, người mua vẫn nên so sánh giá thực tế với iPhone 16 và iPhone Air để xác định mẫu máy có lợi thế rõ ràng nhất về chi phí.
Nên chọn iPhone nào?
Việc lựa chọn iPhone không nên chỉ dựa vào mức giảm giá được công bố. Một mẫu máy giảm nhiều chưa chắc là phương án tiết kiệm nhất nếu không phù hợp với nhu cầu hoặc có chi phí sử dụng lâu dài cao hơn dự kiến.
Nếu ưu tiên thiết kế mỏng nhẹ, iPhone Air là lựa chọn đáng cân nhắc. iPhone 16 phù hợp với người muốn nâng cấp từ các thế hệ cũ; iPhone 13 hướng đến nhóm người cần một thiết bị phục vụ các tác vụ cơ bản; iPhone 17 cân bằng giữa phần cứng mới và giá bán, còn iPhone 17 Pro Max dành cho người cần trải nghiệm cao cấp.

articles.title: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.
The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.
Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.
The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse.
In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

articles.title: Google Gemini 4 agents just beat Minecraft with no human intervention - Engadget
articles.text:
Google Gemini 4 agents just beat Minecraft with no human intervention
Agents split up tasks, warned about threats and even recovered items from dead teammates.
Google's Deepmind "AlphaGo" AI is famous for winning at Go, but the company's latest Gemini AI just mastered a far more complex game. Four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft's final "Ender Dragon" foe with no human intervention by working individually while sharing tips, threats and mistakes, Google researchers revealed in a new paper. The experiment shows how general agentic AI models can now beat complex games, a feat that used to required custom AI software.
To tackle Minecraft, the Gemini 4 team set four AI agents into a sandboxed, randomized Minecraft survival world with a goal to defeat the Ender Dragon. No roles, strategies or game-specific tools were assigned. Each agent controlled a player using the open-source Mineflayer library and coordinated with teammates through in-game chat and shared memory.
During gameplay, agents quickly elected to split up tasks. They warned each about threats, gave lessons and tips, provided coordinates and even recovered items from dead teammates. Each settled into roles: for example, "janesick" made tools, "gyldenia" gathered food and supplies, "auratian" lit a key portal and "bulicame" built Enderman shelters and landed the final blow.
All told, the process took 27.23 hours, with the majority of time spent on the Ender Dragon. "The four agents wrote and ran 2,783 programs, exchanged 229 messages and died 605 times along the way," the team said. A fifth agent called "the Observer" monitored the session as an independent witness, both to check for cheating and to publish live and summary reports. The agents used 1.35 billion input tokens and the final cost was $810 at Gemini's list price or $1,620 at the standard price.
"To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans," the team wrote. "Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day."

articles.title: Maricopa County, Arizona, Is Again Ground Zero of Election Conspiracy Theories
articles.text:
“Maricopa is a very, very dishonest county,” President Donald Trump told reporters last week.
One could be forgiven for thinking that you had time-traveled back to the chaotic weeks and months following the 2020 presidential election, when Arizona's Maricopa County became the focal point for the election denial movement.
But Maricopa, and election deniers, are back. With just over two weeks to go before the midterms, extremist election activists are trying to undermine trust in the voting process and are ramping up their efforts to confuse and scare people. Central to this is to fall back on well-known tropes that have been used in the past, including the idea that Maricopa County is somehow corrupt.
“At this point, people are tuned into Maricopa as a focus of election rumors,” Kate Starbird, cofounder of the Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington, tells WIRED. “Sharpie pens bleeding through ballots in 2020. Tabulator machines not reading ballots in 2022. Maricopa has become a familiar setting, a place where election issues arise or are perceived to arise, and where those issues get wrapped into ‘rigged election’ conspiracy theories.”
No evidence of widespread voter fraud in Maricopa County has ever been found, but in March of this year, the administration refocused attention on the county when the FBI seized dozens of hard drives and servers containing data from the Cyber Ninjas audit. The attention was intensified last week, when Trump told reporters that election officials in the county should “be ashamed of themselves” after 3,000 ballots were mailed early in error.
But the rumors went into overdrive last weekend when We the People USA Alliance, an election-denial group central to the baseless claims about voter fraud in Maricopa County in 2020, posted a video on X with the caption “BUSTED.”
The video shows two Maricopa County employees working late at night on October 7 inside the ballot tabulation center. The post insinuated that they were tampering with equipment by “inserting flash drives into computers … during an active election.”
The post also named a Maricopa County employee, who was previously targeted with similarly unfounded claims and threats back in 2021.
The video quickly racked up over 1 million views, boosted by figures like Kari Lake, the former TV star who is now a senior adviser in the Trump administration, who also boosted claims about election fraud in Maricopa County when she lost races in 2022 and 2024 for governor and the US Senate, respectively.
“More shenanigans at the Maricopa county ballot tabulation center,” Lake wrote on X. “Only through God’s intervention was this even discovered.”
But it wasn’t God who provided the video to the group. Jennifer Liewer, the deputy elections director for communications in Maricopa County tells WIRED that the clip was taken from a nonpublic backup livestream camera that is active but not currently one of the livestream cameras available on the county’s website. A source with knowledge of the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record tells WIRED that members of the We the People group had obtained the IP address for the camera years ago, allegedly allowing them to continue to monitor it. We the People did not respond to a request for comment.
The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors issued a statement last week that debunked the claim, clarifying that the employees were “performing authorized and necessary work to update software and upload election data to a computer terminal that is not connected to the internet or ballot tabulation equipment.”
Unsatisfied with this explanation, Shelby Busch, the founder of We The People USA Alliance and a representative for the Republican National Committee (RNC), then contacted the Maricopa County recorder Justin Heap, who is aligned with Trump. His office then contacted the FBI to investigate the issue, according to Heap’s chief of staff.
The FBI asked an investigator from the Arizona attorney general’s office to investigate, and they quickly concluded there was nothing to investigate, according to a copy of their report seen by 12News. “Election integrity is one of the top priorities of this FBI, and we continue to work around the clock to pursue criminal actors who seek to undermine our system and the rule of law,” the FBI tells WIRED.
The RNC and Busch did not respond to a request for comment.
The FBI’s closed investigation has not quelled the conspiracy theories. On Thursday, Busch appeared on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast repeating claims that something nefarious had happened, and that she had contacted the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice to investigate the matter further.
“Can somebody get involved here?” Bannon replied.
The Justice Department, DHS, and the White House did not respond to a request for comment.
“Election rumors contain the same, or very similar, narrative tropes that make them easily digestible for audiences and remixable for rumor producers,” says Starbird, whose group has created a bingo card of such tropes. “Maricopa County has become a trope, a suspicious setting, for election rumors. It’s a ready-to-use building block for a new rumor or conspiracy theory.”

articles.title: Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
articles.text:
For a very limited time, Sony’s latest high-end noise-canceling earbuds are actually cheaper than their last-gen counterpart, the WF-1000XM5. B&H Photo is selling Sony’s latest WF-1000XM6 in black for an all-time low of $238 ($92 off) at checkout. Other retailers aren’t currently offering a discount on the XM6.
Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
The flagship earbuds now cost about as much as their predecessor.
The XM6 are a solid upgrade over their predecessor and easily amongst the best noise-canceling wireless earbuds on the market. In his review, John Higgins noted that they do a better job of tuning out other people’s conversations than any other earbuds he’s tested. Sony has also improved the bone-conduction sensor and added AI-powered microphones that help keep your voice clear during calls, even in noisy environments.
The XM6 earbuds also deliver clean, balanced sound with impressive bass, raising the bar of what we expect with Sony’s WF-1000XM series. If you prefer to customize your listening experience, Sony’s Sound Connect app offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to adjust how much surrounding noise you hear without removing the earbuds. You can also personalize the touch controls.
The XM6 earbuds support Sony’s LDAC codec, which delivers higher-quality audio from compatible Android devices, too. New in the latest set is a listening mode that makes music sound more like background audio playing in a cafe, allowing you to listen to your favorite music without getting too distracted from whatever you’re doing.

articles.title: Four European carriers to explore a joint satellite spectrum bid
articles.text:
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone have signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for satellite spectrum in Europe. The four companies announced it on Monday in a joint release.
The spectrum is for mobile satellite services (MSS), the radio frequencies that link satellites with mobile devices. The bid would be for its future allocation in Europe. The letter commits the four only to explore a bid, and they gave no timetable.
They said the plan supports the European Commission’s aim of strengthening Europe’s sovereignty, security and resilience in critical connectivity. The four would give every mobile operator open, non-discriminatory access to offer direct-to-device (D2D) services to its customers. The model is meant to foster competition and expand consumer choice, they said.
Ground network, not satellites
The four plan to set up the key ground network in Europe, along with critical coordination and monitoring functions. They will not invest directly in a satellite constellation. The constellation would come from a satellite partner they have yet to select.
They said they aim to bring coverage to underserved areas, make public networks more resilient and protect critical communications. They also want to support the development of a European constellation.
The letter does not replace existing satellite partnerships, the four said. AST SpaceMobile, which counts all four as partners, also announced the letter on Monday. It said it supplies ground stations in Europe through its joint venture, Satellite Connect Europe.
TNW reported in September, citing Bloomberg, that the four carriers were in early talks about a joint satellite venture.
Brussels and the 2 GHz band
In May, the European Union said it was considering a plan to reserve part of the 2 GHz band for European companies. They would use it to offer satellite services. SpaceX criticised the idea, saying it would worsen service in Ukraine, The Verge reported, citing the Financial Times.
In the US, AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon announced their own collaboration earlier this year. It would combine their spectrum in rural areas and dead zones.
Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla, called it a commercial concern, in comments carried by Advanced Television.
“Europe’s operators want to avoid becoming effectively MVNOs for satellite coverage, selling somebody else’s service on somebody else’s terms. Securing MSS spectrum would give them a stronger hand in negotiations.” Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst, Ookla

articles.title: Chuyển gần 400m2 sang đất ở, bị tính tăng hơn 500 triệu: Người phụ nữ thắng kiện
articles.text:
Bị tính tiền đất theo tuyến đường không có lối đi thực tế
Năm 2018, bà Nguyễn Thị Thùy T. nhận chuyển nhượng thửa đất số 126, diện tích 873m2 tại tổ dân phố A, phường B, tỉnh Lâm Đồng. Thời điểm nhận chuyển nhượng, thửa đất được xác định là đất trồng cây hàng năm khác.
Đầu năm 2024, bà T. có nhu cầu chuyển mục đích sử dụng một phần diện tích sang đất ở tại đô thị. Ngày 14/6/2024, UBND thành phố G. ban hành quyết định cho phép bà chuyển mục đích sử dụng 393,5m2 đất.
Ngày 25/6/2024, căn cứ phiếu chuyển thông tin địa chính do Chi nhánh Văn phòng đăng ký đất đai thành phố G. cung cấp, Chi cục Thuế khu vực G1 - Đắk Glong ban hành thông báo yêu cầu bà T. nộp hơn 1,24 tỷ đồng tiền sử dụng đất và hơn 6,5 triệu đồng lệ phí trước bạ.
Thửa đất được xác định thuộc vị trí đường N. để áp dụng giá đất tính nghĩa vụ tài chính.
Không đồng tình, bà T. cho rằng phần đất được chuyển mục đích không tiếp giáp đường N., cũng không có lối đi thực tế ra tuyến đường này mà chỉ tiếp giáp đường M. Việc áp giá đất theo đường N. khiến số tiền sử dụng đất bà phải nộp tăng hơn 500 triệu đồng.
Vì vậy, bà T. khởi kiện, yêu cầu hủy hai thông báo nghĩa vụ tài chính, đồng thời đề nghị cơ quan có thẩm quyền xác định lại vị trí thửa đất, lập phiếu chuyển thông tin địa chính mới và tính lại số tiền phải nộp.
Chi cục Thuế khu vực G1 không đồng ý với yêu cầu khởi kiện. Cơ quan này cho rằng, các thông báo được ban hành đúng quy định, trên cơ sở thông tin do cơ quan đăng ký đất đai cung cấp. Việc xác định vị trí, diện tích và loại đất thuộc trách nhiệm của cơ quan đăng ký đất đai, còn cơ quan thuế căn cứ thông tin được chuyển đến để tính nghĩa vụ tài chính.
Văn phòng đăng ký đất đai tỉnh L. cũng cho biết việc lập phiếu chuyển thông tin địa chính được thực hiện trên cơ sở hồ sơ chuyển mục đích sử dụng đất do cơ quan có thẩm quyền chuyển đến.
Tòa hủy thông báo, yêu cầu xác định lại vị trí thửa đất
Xem xét vụ án, TAND khu vực 6 - Lâm Đồng căn cứ tài liệu hồ sơ, trong đó có văn bản ngày 18/12/2025 của Sở Nông nghiệp và Môi trường tỉnh L., cung cấp thông tin về hiện trạng khu vực tiếp giáp thửa đất.
Theo tài liệu này, tại thời điểm tháng 5/2024, khu vực tiếp giáp thửa đất đã có vỉa hè nhưng phạm vi thu hồi lớn hơn phạm vi vỉa hè và không hình thành tuyến giao thông. Phần đất thuộc phạm vi thu hồi đang là đất trống do Nhà nước quản lý, các phương tiện giao thông không thể đi lại trực tiếp qua khu vực này để ra đường N.
Việc đi lại chỉ có thể thực hiện bằng cách đi bộ qua phần đất thuộc phạm vi thu hồi và vỉa hè. Nếu muốn sử dụng phương tiện giao thông, phải cải tạo và được cơ quan có thẩm quyền cho phép theo quy định.
Tòa án nhận định, tại thời điểm xác định nghĩa vụ tài chính, thửa đất của bà T. không có khả năng tiếp cận giao thông bằng phương tiện ra đường N. Do đó, việc xác định thửa đất thuộc vị trí tuyến đường này để áp dụng giá đất là không phù hợp với hiện trạng thực tế, dẫn đến việc tính nghĩa vụ tài chính chưa chính xác.
Hồ sơ cũng thể hiện thửa đất số 126 được tách thành ba thửa vào ngày 18/10/2024. Trong đó, hai thửa số 2294 và 2295 được chuyển mục đích sử dụng sang đất ở đô thị không giáp đường N.; thửa số 2293 giáp đường N. nhưng không được chuyển mục đích sử dụng đất.
Theo HĐXX, việc xác định vị trí thửa đất để áp dụng giá đất phải căn cứ hiện trạng sử dụng đất và khả năng tiếp cận giao thông thực tế. Trường hợp thửa đất không có lối ra giao thông thực tế thì không thể xác định thuộc vị trí của tuyến đường đó để áp dụng giá đất tương ứng.
Do đó, tòa án chấp nhận một phần yêu cầu khởi kiện của bà T., hủy thông báo nộp tiền sử dụng đất và thông báo nộp lệ phí trước bạ nhà, đất được ban hành ngày 25/6/2024.
Tòa buộc Chi cục Thuế khu vực G1, nay là Thuế cơ sở X., tỉnh Lâm Đồng, ban hành thông báo nộp tiền sử dụng đất mới đối với bà T. theo đúng quy định pháp luật.
Đồng thời, Văn phòng đăng ký đất đai Đ. (nay là tỉnh Lâm Đồng) phải chỉ đạo chi nhánh thực hiện nhiệm vụ công vụ, ban hành phiếu chuyển thông tin địa chính mới để xác định lại vị trí thửa đất, làm căn cứ cho cơ quan thuế xác định nghĩa vụ tài chính.
(Bài viết dựa trên Bản án số 01/2026/HC-ST ngày 31/3/2026 của TAND khu vực 6 - Lâm Đồng).

articles.title: Musk pledges to give 'every kid in America' one of his SpaceX shares | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Elon Musk claims he will give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” in 2027, which would result in a gift worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price of his combination spaceflight and AI company. That’s roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth.
It’s not clear how Musk plans to do this, though he said in a separate post that he wants to give the shares “directly to the public,” and that this will be the “first of many” shares he’ll donate.
President Donald Trump, who Musk spent around $300 million to help elect, has set up bank accounts for children through the Treasury, called Trump Accounts, that can accept stock donations from wealthy donors.
Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Musk’s post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new “public benefit fund,” which it intends to use to make “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” after its upcoming IPO.
On Sunday afternoon, Musk replied directly to Anthropic’s post on X about its new fund, suggesting the company should give “directly to the public” instead.
“This is what I will be doing,” he wrote in another reply four hours later. Then, overnight, he announced his plans to donate SpaceX stock.
There are currently more than 70 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics. Musk owns around 849 million Class A common shares of SpaceX and more than 5.5 billion Class B supervoting shares. He stands to earn many more.
Musk’s philanthropic giving to date has been almost exclusively done through his Musk Foundation. Despite his negative opinions about philanthropy, it’s the fifth-largest private charitable foundation in the U.S. However, a recent review by The Economist showed that a majority of the total money laid out by the Musk Foundation over the years has gone to entities tied to Musk in some way. Nearly 60% has gone to another charity, called The Foundation, run by his money manager, Jared Birchall.

articles.title: What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter? - Engadget
articles.text:
What do all the lights on your Netgear router mean, and which ones actually matter?
Depending on their colors, most of those flashing lights are a good sign.
The front of a Netgear router, like many routers, is dotted with a wide array of lights and symbols. Though some of the symbols like the power indicator are straightforward, the lights themselves can be much less clear. They often vary in color; sometimes they're blinking and other times they're solid. If you've never picked up the manual, deciphering what each of the many lights means doesn't come naturally.
Understanding what each of the indicators on your Netgear router signify is important for troubleshooting, as well as making sure everything is running as it should. Although some lights are usually more important than others, they all serve a purpose. Whether you have a standard router or one of the company's mesh Wi-Fi systems, this is how to better understand what your Netgear device is telling you.
The most important lights on your Netgear router
These are the lights on a router that are generally the most important to pay attention to, as they're indicators of the most impactful stats like power and overall internet connection status.
The power LED
Represented by the typical power symbol, this indicates information about your device's firmware, as well as its power status. Unsurprisingly, this will be off if your router has no power.
- Solid green or white: The router is on and ready.
- Solid amber: The router is turning on.
- Blinking amber: The router's firmware is upgrading, or you pressed the reset button.
- Blinking white: The router's firmware is corrupted.
- Blinking white and amber: The router is in access point mode, which means it's acting as a connection point for other devices instead of handling its normal router functions. Some features like VPN and remote management will be unavailable.
If your router isn't working properly, restart it first. In case it's fully unresponsive, you may need to do a factory reset.
Internet LED
The icon and light with a small circle orbiting a larger one shows your general connection status:
- Off: The router is not connected to a modem; check the Ethernet cable to make sure it's fully inserted and not damaged.
- Solid green or white: The internet connection is ready.
- Solid amber: An Ethernet cable connection to the modem has been detected.
- Blinking white: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
Wi-Fi LED
Represented by a small dot with two curves on each side, this light shows general Wi-Fi traffic.
- Off: The router's Wi-Fi radios are off.
- Solid white: The router's Wi-Fi radios are operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving Wi-Fi traffic.
Other lights on your Netgear router
Further lights on your Netgear router are more useful for specific troubleshooting, or if you're plugging additional devices into the router.
Wi-Fi band LEDS
Every modern router should have lights for the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, as these have long been the standard. For a Wi-Fi 6E model or newer, you'll also see a 6GHz light for that modern band. The lights will differ depending on the bands currently in use, but the lights have the same meanings for each band.
- Off: This particular Wi-Fi radio is off.
- Solid white: The Wi-Fi radio in question is operating.
- Blinking white: The router is sending and/or receiving traffic over the corresponding Wi-Fi radio.
USB LEDs
Your router will have one of these lights for each USB port it includes, represented by the trident USB symbol or the text "USB 3.0."
- Off: No USB device is connected to the port, or the Safely Remove Hardware button was pressed and you're clear to remove the attached device.
- Blinking: A USB device is trying to connect.
- Solid green or white: A USB device is connected and ready to use.
Ethernet LEDs
These are labeled by numbers, with each representing an Ethernet port on the router. The color represents the speed of the connection: white or green for 1 Gbps connections, and amber for slower 100 Mbps or 10 Mbps Ethernet.
- Off: Nothing is connected to the port.
- Solid: A powered-on device is connected to the port.
- Blinking: The port is sending and/or receiving traffic.
WPS LED
Represented by what looks like a router with signals coming out of it, this light indicates the success of a WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) connection, which allows you to add devices to your network without entering the network name and password. For the best router security, you should disable this.
- Off: No WPS connection.
- Blinking: A WPS connection is in progress.
- Solid: The WPS connection was successful.
Reading the lights on a Netgear Orbi mesh system
The lights on Netgear's Orbi Wi-Fi mesh system are minimalist compared to a typical router's, and represent key statuses slightly differently. There's a light in the bottom-front of the device, plus one at the back. The light in the front represents the connection status, while the one at the back is tied to the device's power and firmware.
The front LED lights
- Solid blue light: The connection between the router and satellite is strong.
- Solid amber light: The connection between the router and satellite is OK, but not great.
- Solid magenta light: There's no backhaul connection or no internet connection.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.
The back LED light
- Solid green light: The router and satellite are powered on.
- Solid amber light: The device is rebooting.
- Pulsing amber light: The device is updating its firmware or resetting to factory settings.
- Pulsing red light: Possible hardware issues or connectivity failure.
- No light: The Orbi is not receiving power.

articles.title: Alldocube chính thức ra mắt tại Việt Nam với bộ đôi máy tính bảng

Alldocube chính thức gia nhập thị trường Việt Nam với bộ đôi máy tính bảng iPlay 70E và iPlay 80 Mini Turbo, mang đến trải nghiệm màn hình cùng hiệu năng ấn tượng trong tầm giá.
Thương hiệu uy tín hợp tác cùng các gã khổng lồ công nghệ
Thành lập từ năm 2005, Alldocube đã khẳng định vị thế toàn cầu khi là đối tác chiến lược của Intel và Microsoft. Với cơ sở sản xuất rộng hơn 8.000m² cùng đội ngũ hơn 85 kỹ sư R&D, hãng chuyên phát triển các dòng máy tính bảng và laptop chất lượng, đáp ứng trọn vẹn nhu cầu của người dùng. articles.title: The Story of Billy Evans and ‘Theranos 2.0’
articles.text:
Warning: Light movie spoilers below. Read at your own risk.
Even before becoming the stars of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-buzzed-about new documentary, Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans were a special kind of couple. Holmes “may have ultimately failed to change the world in the way she set out,” Evans wrote in a letter at the time of Holmes’ sentencing in 2022, “but she has undeniably changed mine.” The Theranos founder, in the hardest years of her life, taught her husband “a patience” that he “would have previously dismissed as unnecessary and soft.”
She brought out his inner light, another sentencing letter from a friend of the couple reports: When they returned from a “monthslong camping trip,” Evans “displayed a new level of compassion in his demeanor, a strong sense of intention with his actions, and a heightened desire to listen to and look at others with purpose.” Whatever others might think, Evans was saying, Holmes wasn’t the only one of the pair that had been given a second chance. And they might get a second second chance with Haemanthus, a company that Evans is keen to reassure social media followers is absolutely—most definitely— “not Theranos 2.0.” A person familiar with the business told The Wall Street Journal that Holmes is not involved.
But viewers of You Can See Everything will watch Evans agreeing to the characterization that he and Holmes are making Theranos 2.0. They discuss the trajectory to make a working prototype of something on camera; they talk about collaborating on product ideas from prison. “To meet her, to spend time with her, that was the intention of the film,” the Austin, Texas-based Evans told David Friedberg, a cohost of the podcast All-In. “I haven’t seen it yet. I might think this is the dumbest thing that I have done.”
So who is Evans? And what is he building?
Long before fathering two children—son William and daughter Invicta—with Holmes, Evans grew up in San Diego in one of the city’s more prominent families, heir to midcentury pioneers in the Southern California tourism industry. His grandparents, William and Anne Evans were “two young hoteliers [who] saw the future,” according to the family’s company website, and opened up what would become a popular resort hotel on a mudflat in Mission Bay in 1953. They added a second nearby, and today own a third in La Jolla. This brought generational wealth. The business passed in part to Billy’s father, also named William.
Billy went to the Francis Parker School, one of the most prestigious private schools in the city. “The Evans family is very well respected in San Diego,” said a contemporary of Evans’ who worked for the family as a teenager, but Billy “always a source of drama, would try to fight to start fights.” He had “affluenza” and was “just your classic spoiled rich kid” in a way that was not true of all his relatives. The inner light would come around later. (Evans did not want to be interviewed for the story and did not answer specific questions.)
After graduating from MIT with a bachelor of science in economics, Evans reportedly tried to launch a startup offering medical concierge services. This failed. He then took jobs in a handful of tech companies, including LinkedIn and Luminar Technologies, a self-driving car company. In 2017, at a “Fleet Week charity event” in the Bay Area, the then 25-year-old met Holmes and was “captivated,” he later wrote the judge at her sentencing, “by her childish wonder and authenticity.”
There was some reporting in the early years that the Evans family was not entirely enthused by this courtship, but doubts seemed to have dissipated by the time of the Holmes trial. Billy’s father, William Evans, showed up to the courtroom incognito, under the alias “Hanson,” identifying himself as a kind of mechanic. (He owns an enormous classic car collection.) To journalists, he defended Holmes’ honor. In court, he turned heads by unwrapping a “large Rice Krispies Treat” whose crinkling foil drowned out the judge on the first day of jury selection, NPR reported.
While in the film Evans and Holmes are both shown on fundraising calls, her name doesn’t appear in any of the incorporation documents of Haemanthus, the company Evans founded in 2022. There is little publicly available information on the company; to date, it has released no products and barely has a LinkedIn page, let alone a website. Yet its name can’t help but conjure up Theranos, and, indeed, its stated goal is to bring blood, urine, and saliva testing to American homes in the form of a countertop-size machine, which was more or less the goal of Theranos.
But the technology of Haemanthus seems to be a bit different than that of Theranos. Where the earlier company’s machine hoped to perfect the “miniaturization” of existing diagnostic techniques such that they could fit in a box on a counter, using a very small blood sample, Haemanthus’ machine uses “light.” To employ a cooler word, it uses lasers. The company’s Raman Spectroscopy System, a patent for which was granted January 21, 2025, suggests a machine capable of firing high-power light sources into biological samples and reading the resulting information accurately.
Raman Spectroscopy is a real and promising diagnostic tool and the subject of research since its discovery by, among others, C. V. Raman in 1928. Shine a light source at a material and perhaps one in 1 million photons will shift in frequency in relation to the molecular vibrations of the material it bounced off of. That shift can be measured and analyzed, and a century of work has gone into making this process a little easier and a little more useful, carried out today by specialists at research universities and hospitals.
It may someday be even more useful. WIRED contacted Eric Potma, a professor of chemistry at UC Irvine, to shed some light on the technology. “Given that I act as one of their consultants, I am not sure if it is appropriate for me to delve much further into this,” he wrote back. “All I can say is that from an engineering perspective, they have some interesting ideas that are worth exploring.”
“It is not a technology concept pulled out of thin air, as people may be inclined to think based on the fact that the company is run by Elizabeth's husband (and thus an automatic repeat of the Theranos story),” he continued over email. “My own assessment is that Haemanthus is not Theranos. The engineers at Haemanthus are legit, and they are really trying to push the Raman detection technology into interesting directions.”
The challenges of putting this highly sensitive and difficult diagnostic technique into home appliances able to assess human health markers with a level of accuracy in seconds that will pass regulatory scrutiny—as promised in the company’s promotional materials—are great, though. Last year, The New York Times said that the company had garnered a $3.5 million investment from “friends and family.” It now reports as much as $20 million in funding.
Press accounts of the company’s marketing materials seem to promise investors that the company faces “no regulatory oversight,” in part because the machine would only be developed to test veterinary diseases at first. The New York Times, though, confirmed with the USDA that the agency had regulatory oversight over “vet diagnostics.”
Evans told the Times, which had other questions, that the company was “in stealth” and would remain so: “They aren’t going to find anything associated with the name Haemanthus.” There are a few things out there, among them the patent, but stealth mode continues. The addresses that turn up are mostly connected to private homes in one of Austin’s more desirable neighborhoods, near Barton Springs. Contacted by phone, a few folks who seem likely to be employees of the company declined to talk or even confirm or deny their role.
The desire for “stealth,” though, is a little discordant with the desire to participate in a yearslong documentary project with a graduate of one of Canada’s top business schools. Perhaps it will help raise money: Once the laser system is perfected, the company hopes, according to materials reviewed by the Times, to put the whole thing in a stamp-size wearable device, a research process it told investors will take “three years and $70 million.” Holmes will be reportedly moving from prison to a halfway house next summer. The world may yet be changed.

articles.title: Apple teases MacBook Pro event next week
articles.text:
Apple has sent invites to a second product launch this month, and it’s scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles.
Apple teases MacBook Pro event next week
Following Apple’s smart home-focused launch earlier in the month, Apple is hosting another product event soon.
At the event, Apple is set to announce new Macs and a refreshed iPad Mini, according to Bloomberg. The big announcement is expected to be a new MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen that’s also lighter and has an iPhone-like Dynamic Island. But Apple is also planning on revealing a 14-inch MacBook Pro and a new iMac with the M6 chip, which was recently introduced with the Mac Mini. Apple’s updated iPad Mini will apparently finally get an OLED screen as well and put the selfie cam on the landscape edge.
“Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” Apple’s SVP Marketing Greg Joswiak says in a teaser on X.
This second October launch follows Apple’s smart home-focused “Welcome home” event on October 13th, which included the new HomeView smart home hub, an updated Apple TV 4K and Siri Remote, and a second-generation HomePod Mini.

articles.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world | TechCrunch
articles.text:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto and a major Japanese automotive manufacturer.
Laplace is also working with Nvidia and T-Mobile on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”
“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.
This article has been updated to clarify Laplace’s relationship with Nvidia.

articles.title: Vàng chao đảo, các ‘ông lớn’ vẫn đặt cược mốc 5.000 USD
articles.text:
Sau ba phiên giảm liên tiếp, kim loại quý bất ngờ bật tăng hơn 65 USD, đóng cửa phiên 15/10 (giờ Mỹ) tại 4.170,48 USD/ounce, tương đương mức tăng 1,60% - phiên tăng mạnh nhất trong nhiều tuần.
Điều gì đã kéo vàng lên? Câu trả lời đến từ lợi suất trái phiếu kho bạc Mỹ kỳ hạn 10 năm, vốn đã giảm mạnh 12,8 điểm cơ bản xuống 5,062%, kéo dài đà hạ nhiệt sau khi chạm đỉnh nhiều tuần. Chỉ số USD (DXY) cũng giảm 0,48% xuống 102,06 điểm trong sáng 16/10, làm giảm chi phí cơ hội nắm giữ vàng - thứ vốn không sinh lời.
Nhưng theo giới phân tích, đây có thể chỉ là nhịp hồi kỹ thuật, không phải đảo chiều xu hướng.
Nghịch lý "lạm phát nóng - việc làm lạnh": Fed đang bị kẹt
Điều khiến câu chuyện vàng trở nên khó đoán chưa từng có chính là bức tranh kinh tế Mỹ đang ở thế "tiến thoái lưỡng nan".
Theo Cục Thống kê Lao động Mỹ (BLS), chỉ số giá sản xuất (PPI) tháng 9 tăng 1,3% so với tháng trước - mức tăng mạnh nhất kể từ tháng 3/2022 và 6,3% so với cùng kỳ, vượt xa dự báo 5,3%. Chỉ số giá tiêu dùng (CPI) cũng không kém cạnh khi tăng 0,6% theo tháng và 3,7% theo năm, cao hơn dự báo 3,6%.
Theo phân tích của Tân Hoa Xã Kinh tế, "thủ phạm" chính là giá năng lượng. Giá xăng tăng 9,1% trong tháng 9, đóng góp hơn một nửa mức tăng của CPI. Giá dầu diesel từng chạm mức cao lịch sử 6,528 USD/gallon.
Giá dầu Brent trung bình tháng 9 đạt 102 USD/thùng, tăng 51% so với cùng kỳ, chủ yếu do căng thẳng địa chính trị tại Trung Đông leo thang.
Nhưng nghịch lý nằm ở đây: thị trường lao động Mỹ lại đang “lạnh” dần. Báo cáo việc làm phi nông nghiệp tháng 9 chỉ ghi nhận 29.000 việc làm mới, thấp hơn rất nhiều so với dự báo khoảng 90.000. Số đơn xin trợ cấp thất nghiệp lần đầu ở mức 199.000, dấu hiệu cho thấy doanh nghiệp đang thắt lưng buộc bụng.
Thị trường phân vân chưa từng thấy. Xác suất Fed tăng lãi suất trong tháng 10 chỉ còn khoảng 29-34%, nhưng xác suất tăng vào tháng 12 vẫn ở mức cao trên 80%. Nói cách khác, Fed có thể sẽ "án binh bất động" trong ngắn hạn, nhưng chưa chắc đã buông tha cho thị trường.
Dự báo thận trọng của các 'ông lớn'
Theo phân tích của UBS công bố gần đây, phần lớn tác động từ việc thị trường định giá lại lập trường "diều hâu" của Fed đã được phản ánh vào giá vàng.
UBS nhận định vùng 4.140-4.200 USD/ounce đang là khu vực tích lũy, và 3.990-4.030 USD/ounce là vùng hỗ trợ then chốt cần theo dõi. UBS duy trì lộ trình giá: 4.600 USD vào tháng 12/2026, 5.000 USD vào tháng 3/2027 và 5.400 USD vào tháng 9/2027.
Bà Amy Gower - Giám đốc chiến lược kim loại và khai khoáng Morgan Stanley, xác định 4.000 USD/ounce là vùng hỗ trợ mạnh mẽ và dự báo vàng sẽ vượt 5.000 USD/ounce vào nửa cuối năm 2027.
Morgan Stanley nhấn mạnh ba trụ cột hỗ trợ: nhu cầu vật chất từ ngân hàng trung ương (đặc biệt Trung Quốc và Ba Lan), khả năng can thiệp vào thị trường trái phiếu dài hạn để hạ lợi suất và triển vọng hạ nhiệt căng thẳng Trung Đông kéo giá dầu đi xuống.
HSBC vừa hạ dự báo giá vàng trung bình năm 2026 xuống 4.490 USD/ounce và năm 2027 xuống 4.825 USD/ounce, nhưng nhấn mạnh rằng nếu vàng giảm về hoặc dưới 4.000 USD, lực mua từ ngân hàng trung ương sẽ gia tăng đáng kể, tạo lực đỡ quan trọng. Đáng chú ý, đây là dự báo giá trung bình năm, không phải mục tiêu cuối năm.
Theo phân tích của Deutsche Bank, ông Daniel Ghali - Giám đốc nghiên cứu kim loại nhận định vàng đang ở trạng thái "quá bán và được nắm giữ ở mức thấp", với cấu trúc vị thế "gần như tái diễn kịch bản năm 2022". Ông cho rằng tốc độ mua vàng của khu vực chính thức đã tăng hơn gấp đôi so với năm 2022, và đây là "thời điểm rất tốt để phân bổ vàng".
Bank of America, trong báo cáo ngày 12/10, tỏ ra thận trọng hơn khi dự báo giá vàng trung bình quý IV/2026 ở mức 4.000 USD/ounce, cho rằng vàng khó duy trì ổn định trên ngưỡng này trong ba tháng tới. Tuy nhiên, BofA dự báo giá vàng trung bình năm 2027 tăng lên 4.813 USD/ounce.
'Bàn tay vô hình' của các ngân hàng trung ương
Theo thông tin Ngân hàng Nhân dân Trung Quốc (PBOC) công bố ngày 7/10, dự trữ vàng của Trung Quốc tính đến cuối tháng 9/2026 đạt 77,47 triệu ounce (khoảng 2.410 tấn), tăng 740.000 ounce so với tháng 8, đánh dấu tháng tăng thứ 23 liên tiếp.
Đây không phải động thái ngẫu nhiên, mà là một phần trong chiến lược dài hạn nhằm giảm phụ thuộc vào đồng USD.
Dòng vốn ETF cũng cho thấy nhà đầu tư dài hạn vẫn kiên nhẫn. Theo dữ liệu của Hội đồng Vàng Thế giới (WGC), các quỹ ETF vàng toàn cầu hút ròng khoảng 10 tỷ USD trong tháng 9, đưa tổng dòng vốn vào quý III lên mức kỷ lục 31 tỷ USD. Tổng lượng vàng nắm giữ của các quỹ tăng thêm 67 tấn, lên 4.256 tấn vào cuối tháng 9.
Về địa chính trị, căng thẳng tại Trung Đông tiếp tục là "chất xúc tác" cho nhu cầu trú ẩn. Lực lượng Houthi gia tăng các cuộc tấn công nhằm vào các cơ sở năng lượng của Saudi Arabia, trong khi một tàu chở dầu bị bốc cháy tại vùng biển phía đông eo biển Hormuz, đẩy giá dầu Brent lên trên 106 USD/thùng.
CCB Futures đánh giá, các yếu tố cấu trúc như phi đô la hóa, nợ công Mỹ leo thang và mua vàng của ngân hàng trung ương vẫn chưa bị đảo ngược.
Vùng 3.800-4.200 USD/ounce có thể là khu vực đáy trung hạn, tức giới đầu tư có thể coi các nhịp điều chỉnh về vùng này là cơ hội tích lũy chiến lược, thay vì tín hiệu đảo chiều của xu hướng tăng dài hạn.

articles.title: Apple sets 28 October event, expected to bring its first touchscreen Mac
articles.text:
Apple has confirmed a “Pro and tell” event in Los Angeles on 28 October. Bloomberg reports it will show its first touchscreen MacBook Pro with an OLED screen, an entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, a new iMac and an OLED iPad mini. Apple has not confirmed any products.
Apple will hold a launch event in Los Angeles on 28 October under the tagline “Pro and tell,” the company confirmed on Monday. Press releases are expected at 10am Pacific Time, followed by hands-on sessions for media.
Apple has not said what it will show. But the event is expected to bring its first touchscreen MacBook, Bloomberg reported. Mark Gurman had earlier said the launch was planned for 27 October.
According to Bloomberg, the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models will have OLED touchscreens and a Dynamic Island, the cut-out at the top of the iPhone screen. They are also said to be much lighter than current models.
Apple is also expected to add a cheaper 14-inch MacBook Pro with its M6 chip, and a refreshed iMac. Both are set to keep their current designs, Bloomberg said. Apple launched the M6, its first 2nm chip, in the Mac mini in August.
The fourth product is likely an iPad mini with an OLED screen, better speakers and a moved front camera, 9to5Mac reported, citing Gurman. Bloomberg first reported the OLED iPad mini in July, with an October launch target.
The touchscreen Mac is part of a wider plan to overhaul every Mac over the next year. Apple has long rejected touchscreens on laptops, saying macOS is designed for a mouse and trackpad.
“Pro and tell” will be Apple’s third launch this autumn and the second under chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on 1 September. It follows the HomeView smart home display, a second HomePod mini and a new Apple TV, Bloomberg said.
Ternus’s first event in September brought the foldable iPhone Duo, which goes on sale this Friday.

articles.title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India's hospital economics | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.
The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.
Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.
That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.
Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.
“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.
Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary.
“We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch.
Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment.
Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes.
The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.
Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison.
Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).
Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said.
Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show.
In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting.
Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time. The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said.
Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable.
“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

articles.title: How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else
articles.text:
Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of the fraud-ridden blood-test company Theranos, made her national press debut in The Wall Street Journal in 2013. The article—“A Drop of Blood, an Instant Diagnosis”—wasn’t a science story, or even a business story. It ran in the Opinion section, by a writer on the Journal’s editorial board named Joseph Rago, winner of a Pulitzer Prize for critiques of the Affordable Care Act.
He wrote that he was impressed by the prospect of individuals having more direct control of their health care; no less an eminence than former secretary of state George Shultz, a Theranos board member, had told Rago that Holmes was the next Steve Jobs or Bill Gates.
By 2014, Holmes was the youngest woman billionaire ever, and the mid-2010s were electric with tech-industry success stories—the iPhone, Tesla, Airbnb, Twitter. I was an editor at WIRED back then, and Theranos-as-presented felt very WIRED. It looked like evidence that a Silicon Valley approach to innovation would work in every industry, including medicine. And at the magazine that first published the idea of the “quantified self,” Theranos’ pitch validated the notion that individuals could take charge of their own health with innovative tech and access to data.
One of my colleagues, an editor named Caitlin Roper, saw a story in Theranos and in Holmes, but no one was sure what shape it should take. The executive editor suggested Roper just go talk to Holmes and see what was what. The result was an influential long-form Q&A headlined “One Drop, Infinite Data: How Elizabeth Holmes Built a Better Blood Test.” Because print magazines move with the agility and speed of a post-Panamax cargo ship, the story didn’t run until the March 2014 issue.
Over the next few months, other publications followed. Fortune put Holmes on the cover. The New Yorker did a profile. In October 2015, Inc. put her on the cover, calling her “the next Steve Jobs”—and a couple of weeks later, The Wall Street Journal did another article on Theranos, by the reporter John Carreyrou. The headline was deceptively humble: “Theranos Has Struggled with Blood Tests.”
Uh-oh.
The speedy and accurate blood tests were fake, the innovative tech didn’t exist, and Walgreens, a major partner, terminated its deal with Theranos. It was a grift. A new documentary film, out this week, follows Holmes in the weeks leading up to her incarceration.
Get a bunch of old WIRED editors together these days and it doesn’t take more than one drink before we start asking each other whether we enabled the worst parts of the tech world’s rise to power. Sometimes it seems like every antichrist-lecturing, panopticon-building, machine-god-bothering weirdo with $100 billion and a government contract made his debut in our pages. So, with Theranos and Holmes back in the news, the current administration at WIRED wondered what we were thinking back then.
It was a long time ago. I called Caitlin.
As always, we were looking for good stories. “I was interested in this female founder, but also the idea that her actual goal was disruption of health care, that there could be more transparency and reduced costs,” says Roper, who today is executive producer for scripted film and TV at The New York Times. “I was going through some medical stuff at the time and having constant blood tests, and I was curious about what this could do.”
Roper got a go-ahead to report and write something, execution to be determined. In the house jargon: Green light, format TK. She and I talked it through separately. “The conversation I remember with you, which I thought of many years later, was looking at the board of directors, her board, which was just completely batshit. It had military figures and government officials, and just seemed very odd,” Roper says. “You said there was something weird about that. It raised your suspicious hackles.”
It did—a few of us thought we saw hints of red flags. The company hadn’t published any peer-reviewed data. Colleagues had heard unconfirmable rumors of shenanigans inside the company. But that didn’t mean it wasn’t a story. We’d just have to figure out how to handle all that. WIRED had been, in years past, overly credulous, especially of scientific claims. But primarily WIRED covered innovation and stuff that sounded futuristic. This felt like it qualified.
“I remember that with dramatic irony, looking back,” Roper says.
Holmes agreed to an interview, and Roper went down to the Valley, to Theranos’ offices. She was only the second reporter to be there, and she got the performance that Holmes would become famous for. “There’s a lot of weird things about her. She was speaking in this strange, low voice. She was wearing a Steve Jobs outfit—black turtleneck,” Roper says. “She seemed like she was very precisely trying to project something.” (That first WSJ story ran with an illustrated caricature; WIRED shot a photo, professionally styled, of Holmes in her signature look.)
They spent an hour talking. Roper got her blood drawn, a tiny pinprick from the tip of her finger. “I said, ‘I’d love to see the box, can I follow my blood sample?’” Roper says. “They said, absolutely not.” Company reps implied it was a health-and-safety issue.
Instead, Holmes took Roper to the Palo Alto Walgreens, one of the few where Theranos had actually set up shop. “That part seemed like a snow job,” Roper says. “It was clear even from my own basic research that it hadn’t rolled out.” The booth at Walgreens was not in service. Holmes told her the company was going to open Walgreens labs across the Southwest.
Roper’s blood results came back. “The panel they took was similar to a panel I’d just had. I looked at them, and they matched,” Roper says. That seemed roughly confirmatory, at the time. It’s impossible to know now how it pulled that off, but later it turned out Theranos maintained a fully kitted-out lab in its Palo Alto offices, in addition to the lab for the company’s supposed new tech.
Interview done, Roper drove back up to San Francisco, to WIRED. “It didn’t feel like there was a feature to do,” she says. The Walgreens stuff wasn’t happening yet; it was too hard to report out how the technology worked. What was hard, in retrospect, was validation. Roper and the bosses weren’t sure that investment money from bold-faced names made up for an absence of hard scientific evidence.
So Roper wrote it up as an interview—a Q&A. “It seemed more like an interesting founder story,” she says. Roper asked every hard question, and got answers. They just turned out to be lies. But Roper acknowledges some cracks in the story’s origin. “If she had not been a woman, I would have been less motivated. That was part of what compelled me,” she says. “I felt sympathetic to the idea of her outfit and her weirdness, because I related to the idea that she was passing in some way in that environment, needing to assert herself.”
It’s tempting to see in that a DEI-run-amok story. It isn’t. All of us at WIRED were trying to wrestle with sexism in the world we covered, and at our magazine. Holmes’ board was all non–Silicon Valley types—was that because venture investors and scientists had identified her as a bad risk, or was it because Silicon Valley venture capitalists don’t support women founders?
Just a month after Roper’s Q&A ran, a team of researchers at the Harvard Business School and MIT Sloan School published a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that investors were far more likely to fund the same pitch if it came from a man than if it came from a woman—and that conventionally attractive men did even better. Today, roughly 75 percent of venture investors are men, and the proportions were worse a decade ago. There’s even research showing that male venture investors are more likely to promote women to partner if the men have daughters. Roper and WIRED were trying to fight that tide and ran aground on a grifter instead.
“Partially, yes, it’s a woman founder, and that’s a nice change of pace. It would’ve been nice if you guys could have beaten John Carreyrou and figured it out,” says Dave Karpf, an associate professor at George Washington University who has read every issue of WIRED and uses them to teach a class about Silicon Valley’s visions of the future. “But it wasn’t a new, untested claim. It was an active fraud.”
It’s fair to imagine a timeline where WIRED dug in deeper and was more critical, or at least didn’t further drive the hype cycle. “That story and the way we photographed her was absolutely fuel to lauding her and drawing attention,” Roper says. “I do feel partially responsible for that.”
We probably were, but I’m not sure WIRED’s Q&A was any more or less credulous than stories other magazines did. I know I sound defensive here, but even WIRED’s rigorous fact-check process wasn’t designed to unmask fraud. We all got got; it’s easy to see red flags when they’re in the rearview mirror. Was it weird to believe a 19-year-old college dropout had noticed something about pathology and microfluidics no one else had? Sure, but as Karpf points out, the system valorizes those kinds of iconoclasts. Steve Jobs was a dropout, man!
“If she had done all the graduate work, she wouldn’t have been nearly as fundable. They would just find someone else to tell them the stories they want to fund,” Karpf says. “It’s the people promoting it who, I think, have a bunch of answering to do.”
In 2019, as Sam Altman was leaving his role leading the tech incubator Y Combinator to become CEO of OpenAI, he wrote a blog post extolling the virtue in founders with “too much self belief … almost to the point of delusion.” Venture investors will tell you they invest in people as much as ideas, and the ideas are sometimes early-days, or half-baked. The system encourages exaggeration—right up to the line of deception. It can favor charismatic hucksters. If Theranos’ technology didn’t quite work yet, well, that’s a core tenet of Silicon Valley: Fake it till you make it.
And for a long time, WIRED helped. The magazine touted big ideas, and sometimes those ideas turned out to be dumb. Sometimes we were too early; sometimes we were wrong. Pitch meetings for stories big and small were a bit of a Thunderdome, actually. Eventually we developed some heuristics to encode skepticism in the process. For architecture stories, renders weren’t enough—ground had to have been broken. Physical objects had to exist in physical space; reporters had to be able to visit a thing. A flying car had to, you know, fly. In stories about new drugs or medical devices, the gating rule became “phase 3 trials or get the fuck out.”
Today, every responsible tech journalist has had to don new kinds of armor to prepare for the future that WIRED helped create. It’s possible to marvel at robot cars navigating cities as if driven by ghosts—while acknowledging the ways they sometimes fail, are often remote-piloted by humans, and pose new questions about regulating Big Tech. It’s possible to be awed by generative artificial intelligence’s capabilities while also interrogating the motives and practices of the companies that build it. And, yes, the personal politics of tech trillionaires matter when they’re donating more than a quarter of a billion dollars to support one political party over another. All of that was probably WIRED’s responsibility back then; it’s everyone’s responsibility now.
The tech business hates all that, reasonably. Not rarely, some longtime Silicon Valley dude will learn I spent most of my career at WIRED and say something like, “What happened to that place? I miss the old, optimistic WIRED.”
But you know, in the same issue of the magazine that carried the Holmes Q&A, another of our colleagues, Bill Wasik, wrote an opinion piece touted on the cover as “Silicon Valley’s Douchebag Problem.” Wasik, today the science editor at The New York Times, wrote then that dead-eyed misbehavior in pursuit of profit would kill tech’s magical status. Peter Thiel–derived ideas about secession and business models that relied on surveillance capitalism risked a backlash that would burn it all down, Wasik warned. The Valley and its toys, he wrote, would end up “a punch line—a hallucination of a future that no one believes in anymore.”
Science and tech journalism have to be about more than investors and returns. The future is too important; the stakes are too high. Case in point: As part of Joseph Rago’s reporting on Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos, he got his finger pricked. Rago’s blood test results were back “by the time I walked out the door,” he wrote. “(Phew: all clear.)” Four years later, Rago, 34, died alone in his New York apartment.
The city medical examiner said the cause of his death was sarcoidosis, a rare (and rarely fatal), hard-to-diagnose inflammatory disorder. Doctors usually figure it out by excluding other possibilities. Rago didn’t even know he had the disease. But among its signs are elevated levels of vitamin D and angiotensin-converting enzyme. Maybe an honest blood test would have spotted it.
