articles.title: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
articles.text:
Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to provide up to 960 megawatts of carbon-free energy for both the regional power grid and Amazon’s data centers.
Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
The proposed nuclear plant would provide 960 megawatts to power the grid — and Amazon’s data centers.
No timeline for construction or operation has been announced for the facility, which Amazon says “could” create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The facility in Indiana is targeting to build 12 Xe-100 SMR’s, an advanced (but unproven) reactor that’s still undergoing development and licensing. These reactors can be cooled using either air, water, or a hybrid solution of both, which Amazon says should allow them to be deployed in water-constrained regions without impacting water demand in local communities.
Indiana also happens to be home to a famously expensive and uncompleted energy project called the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant. It was abandoned half-finished in 1983 after $2.5 billion had already been sunk into it, and has been under continued demolition since 2008. Terms for Amazon’s agreement in Fairbanks haven’t been disclosed, so we can’t compare the cost between the facilities.
This marks the second nuclear energy project that Amazon and X-energy are collaborating on, with the collective goal of working with regional utilities to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity in the US by 2039. In October last year, Amazon shared an early preview of its first planned nuclear plant, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. That project is similarly set to build 12 advanced reactors and create local jobs, but construction isn’t expected to start until the end of this decade.
Amazon is one of several tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, and Google, that are exploring their own nuclear energy projects to power AI data centers. Investing in energy grid infrastructure was also one of the commitments that Amazon outlined in a lengthy blog post earlier this month that aimed to sway some of the growing negativity around data center projects, though it’ll be many years before anyone — including Amazon — can reap the benefits of these new facilities.

articles.title: Amazon's TorchNeuron lets PyTorch code run on AWS Trainium chips
articles.text:
Amazon has launched TorchNeuron, an open-source backend that lets PyTorch code run on its Trainium AI chips with a one-line change. It goes into public beta on 20 October under the Apache 2.0 licence and supports Trainium2 and Trainium3. Some PyTorch features are not yet supported.
Amazon has launched TorchNeuron, a tool that lets developers run their existing PyTorch code on its Trainium AI chips without rewriting it, the company said on Monday. PyTorch is the most widely used software framework for building AI models.
TorchNeuron will go into public beta on 20 October at the PyTorch Conference in San Jose, according to a PyTorch blog post by Amazon engineers. It will be open source under the Apache 2.0 licence and supports Trainium2 and Trainium3.
Until now, moving AI code to a new chip often meant months of rewriting and testing. With TorchNeuron, developers point their code at Trainium by changing a single device setting, Amazon said.
In a demo, Amazon ran the same training script on a standard chip and on Trainium, and said the model learned at the same rate on both. The tool plugs into PyTorch’s built-in system for adding new hardware, so standard testing and scaling tools still work.
However, the first release has gaps. It does not yet support some PyTorch features, such as dynamic input shapes, and about 22,000 PyTorch tests are skipped, according to the PyTorch blog post.
Early users include voice AI startups Cartesia and Deepgram, as well as the Lieber Institute for Brain Development, which uses it in drug research. Hugging Face has also added Trainium support to its AI tools. Uber recently signed up to use the chips in an AWS expansion deal.
The launch is part of Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, whose chips and CUDA software dominate AI computing. In April, chief executive Andy Jassy said Amazon’s custom chip business could be worth $50B, and Amazon now says it has passed a $25B annual revenue run rate.
One of TorchNeuron’s launch partners is Decart, an AI chip software startup that Amazon was reported to be in talks to buy.

articles.title: A successful AI pilot doesn’t mean your AI strategy is working
articles.text:
Launching an AI pilot is relatively straightforward. But integrating it reliably and at scale into business operations is a far greater challenge. McKinsey’s global 2026 survey found that only 37% of respondents said AI had improved their company’s earnings, unchanged from the previous year. Yet eight in ten said AI had helped them become more productive at work.
An AI tool may work well during a small test, when the task is simple and the data is clean. But using it across a company brings new challenges. It must integrate with existing software, comply with data access and security requirements, and have a clear process for handling failures. Someone must also take responsibility for its performance. Meeting these requirements means coordinating across IT, operations, finance, and risk teams.
Costs create another challenge. Companies are used to setting budgets for software projects and estimating staff time. AI costs can be harder to predict. They depend on how much information the system processes, which model it uses, and how often people use it. Without a clear estimate, finance teams may struggle to judge whether a project is worth the investment.
Cost each use case first
Zacharie Lahmi, founder of Ellis Partners, recommends that companies assess AI opportunities one business process at a time. He has ten years of experience in technology, including work helping launch monday.com in France. His approach focuses on estimating the cost and resources required for each use case before testing it.
“Companies need to understand the cost of a use case and the resources it will require. The return-on-investment discussion should happen before the pilot, not after.” Zacharie Lahmi, founder of Ellis Partners
Every AI test needs clear goals and a plan for when things go wrong. Lahmi recommends setting measurable targets for usage, maintenance costs, and errors.
“Useful pilots are the ones we really want to see in production. We should agree on success criteria beforehand, so there is no debate after the pilot about whether it worked.” Zacharie Lahmi
Look beyond sales and marketing
Lahmi also urges companies to look beyond sales and marketing when choosing AI projects. While these functions offer benefits that may be easier to link to revenue, he believes everyday operational processes can offer greater opportunities.
“The most boring operational tasks, the core processes of your industry, are the ones you should be thinking about with AI. Ask yourself how you can fundamentally change the way your industry operates, rather than simply maximizing short-term gains.” Zacharie Lahmi
Some enterprise AI projects remain in testing for several months, according to Lahmi. Often, nobody has defined what the project must achieve to justify wider use. He recommends assessing each AI project based on the business problem it would solve.
“Companies should then weigh the expected benefits against the effort required to implement it and the time it would take to see results. A smaller project that delivers results quickly may be a better starting point than a larger one.” Zacharie Lahmi
He suggests examining everyday business operations, too. Improving a process can change how a company works, rather than simply helping employees complete tasks faster.
Size changes the pace
Company size also affects how easily AI projects can be introduced and adjusted. Lahmi notes that smaller businesses often have fewer layers of approval, allowing them to make decisions and change direction more quickly. Large enterprises may face more hurdles because changes can affect multiple teams and existing systems.
Regardless of company size, businesses might need to assess whether an AI system delivers the results they expected. They can track how much time it saves, whether it reduces mistakes, and what it costs to maintain. These measures can help leaders decide whether to continue with a project, make changes, or stop it altogether. A successful demonstration alone might not be enough to justify wider adoption.
From experiment to dependable tool
For stakeholders, the final litmus test for enterprise AI is not just doing the same thing faster, but fundamentally changing how value is created. Launching more pilot projects does not necessarily mean a company is making progress. Each project needs a clear goal and a realistic budget, along with limits on the risks the business is willing to accept.
Companies can review performance after launch and ensure someone has the authority to pause and audit a system if problems arise. These steps can help turn AI experiments into tools that businesses can depend on.

articles.title: Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
articles.text:
Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available from Amazon for $779.99 (originally $899) for the past couple of weeks. However, at $649 it’s a much more tempting price.
Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
At $649, it’s a much better deal. However, the new, faster M6 version is only $130 more.
The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024, and was an incredible value. Given that this sale price makes it just $50 more than the original price instead of $200, it’s a good time to buy if you want to spend as little as possible on a modern Mac desktop.
Aside from some impressive generational leaps in processing power, you aren’t missing out on a ton by skipping the M6 model and opting for the M4. Their design and ports are nearly identical, and with either model you’ll need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam, etc. If you’re on the fence and can’t decide between the M4 and M6 models, I suggest checking out my colleague Antonio’s review of the M6 Mac Mini. The newer model might be well worth the extra $130 cost.
Read our review of the M4 Mac Mini and the M6 Mac Mini
More Verge-approved deals
- Today brought a big discount to LG’s C6 OLEDs lineup, particularly its bigger models. The 55-inch model is $999.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco (previously $1,399.99), costing a little less than the 42- and 48-inch configurations. The price hasn’t gone below $1,299.99 before, so it’s a good time to consider an upgrade. The 65-inch model is cheaper than before, too. Previously $1,699.99, but normally selling for $1,500 or so, you can grab the larger version for $1,399.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco. If you have a big room and budget, the 77-inch LG C6H that, like the 48-inch version, has a tandem OLED panel that offers more brightness and better colors, is $1,999.99, down from $2,499.99.
- For $499.99, you can grab a 14-inch HP OmniBook 3 during Best Buy’s deal of the day that has a 2K OLED screen, a capable Snapdragon X ARM processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. This seems like a fantastic option for anyone on a budget. Its Snapdragon processor can run most x86 Windows 11 apps without much issue, and it’s just a rarity to get these kinds of specs — from the OLED screen to the RAM amount — at $500. My colleague Antonio reviewed the 16-inch version that cuts some corners in the screen department compared to this 14-inch model.
- It’s time to get spooky if you haven’t already planned your run of games for Halloween. The spectacular Silent Hill 2 remake is down to $21.34 on Steam for PC via Fanatical, a third-party site I’ve shopped from numerous times. If you’re alright with spending more, Resident Evil Requiem is one of Capcom’s several great 2026 games, and it’s $20 off at Amazon on all platforms, costing $49.99.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 19/10: Thế giới hạ nhiệt, xăng trong nước chờ tuần mới
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Mở cửa phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này (19/10), giá dầu thế giới có xu hướng đi xuống, sau khi tăng mạnh ở tuần trước.
Dữ liệu từ Oilprice cho hay, vào lúc 7h08' ngày 19/10 (giờ Việt Nam), giá dầu Brent được niêm yết ở mức 108,1 USD/thùng, giảm 1,58% so với phiên liền trước. Còn giá dầu WTI được giao dịch ở mức 100,7 USD/thùng, hạ 0,71% so với phiên liền trước.
Trong tuần trước, giá dầu thế giới tăng mạnh. Tính chung trong cả tuần qua, giá dầu Brent tăng gần 5%, trong khi dầu WTI tăng hơn 10%.
Giá dầu Brent đóng cửa tuần qua ở mức 109,9 USD/thùng, còn giá dầu WTI kết tuần trước ở mức 101,4 USD/thùng.
Giá dầu thế giới đi xuống trong đầu phiên giao dịch 19/10 sau thông tin Tổng thống Donald Trump sẽ tạm dừng các biện pháp trừng phạt Nga để phân tích tác động với nền kinh tế toàn cầu.
Ngày 18/10, TASS đưa tin, Tổng thống Mỹ Donald Trump cho biết ông dự định đưa ra một quyết định quan trọng liên quan đến các biện pháp trừng phạt Nga. Ông khẳng định bước đi này sẽ đem lại lợi ích thiết thực cho nước Mỹ và cộng đồng quốc tế.
Phát biểu trước các phóng viên tại dinh thự Mar-a-Lago ở bang Florida, ông Donald Trump tiết lộ công chúng sẽ sớm được thông tin về quyết định này. Ông nhấn mạnh đây sẽ là một quyết sách đúng đắn và tích cực cho nước Mỹ nói riêng cũng như cục diện chung trên trường quốc tế.
Trước đó, Ngoại trưởng Mỹ Marco Rubio thông báo ông Donald Trump đã thiết lập khung thời gian 60 ngày để rà soát và đánh giá toàn diện hậu quả tiềm ẩn từ các đòn trừng phạt Nga, bao gồm mức thuế bổ sung áp lên các quốc gia đối tác cùng những tác động đối với nền kinh tế Mỹ và toàn cầu.
Tuy nhiên, những lo ngại về nguồn cung cũng gia tăng khi các cuộc tấn công xung quanh eo biển Hormuz leo thang trong nhiều ngày qua, sau khi Iran tuyên bố tăng cường các cuộc tấn công để đáp trả việc Mỹ phong tỏa các cảng của nước này và các lệnh trừng phạt khắc nghiệt hơn được áp đặt vào tháng trước.
Trong một báo cáo công bố vào ngày 15/10, các chuyên gia tại công ty dữ liệu và phân tích thị trường hàng hóa Kpler cho biết: "Các cuộc tấn công gia tăng từ phía Iran đã khiến lưu lượng dầu thô từ vùng Vịnh sụt giảm mạnh".
Các nhà phân tích nhận định rằng nếu không có một thỏa thuận chính trị toàn diện, quá trình phục hồi lưu lượng dầu qua eo biển Hormuz sẽ diễn ra chậm chạp và không đồng đều.
Dù giá dầu có xu hướng giảm trong phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này nhưng nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung vẫn có thể khiến thị trường biến động mạnh trong thời gian tới.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (19/10) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 15/10, giá xăng E5RON92 hạ 732 đồng/lít, giá bán lẻ không cao hơn 26.971 đồng/lít.
Trong khi giá xăng E10RON95-III được điều chỉnh giảm tới 1.225 đồng/lít, xuống mức 27.029 đồng/lít.
Cùng xu hướng, giá dầu diesel 0.05S được điều chỉnh giảm nhẹ 22 đồng/lít, xuống mức giá không cao hơn 29.106 đồng/lít.
Trái lại, giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 1.043 đồng/kg, lên tối đa 22.135 đồng/kg.
Trong chiều 15/10, Tập đoàn Xăng dầu Việt Nam (Petrolimex) tiến hành giảm thêm 300 đồng/lít hoặc kg đối với các mặt hàng xăng dầu so với mức giá bán tối đa được công bố trong kỳ điều hành 15/10.
Tổng công ty Dầu Việt Nam (PVOIL) cũng giảm 350 đồng/lít đối với hai loại xăng và dầu diesel từ 0h ngày 16/10.
Theo dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính đang tiếp tục theo dõi sát diễn biến thị trường để thông báo giá xăng dầu phù hợp với diễn biến thị trường và kịp thời đề xuất Chính phủ, Thủ tướng các giải pháp bình ổn giá xăng dầu.

articles.title: Insta360 Luna Gimbal Camera Gives You the Steady Shots Your Audience Deserves
articles.text:
Excellent gimbal and subject tracking. Detachable screen with recording controls. Superior image quality compared to action cameras and smartphones. The Ultra's dual lenses allow for more versatility.
TIRED
Small screen makes accessing advanced settings somewhat fiddly. Non-replaceable battery.
Not long ago, the idea of a compact, capable, and affordable camera gimbal seemed unfathomable. But then DJI pioneered this space with the Osmo Mobile, a gimbal for filming with your phone, and the Osmo Pocket, a gimbal-camera combo that's proved extremely popular. Now, Insta360 has joined the party with two competing gimbal cameras, the Insta360 Luna Ultra and Luna Pro.
You'd be forgiven for mistaking these Insta360 cameras for the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 and 4 Pro. In fact, the two companies are currently butting heads in a US court over these and other cameras. Oddly, given the lawsuit, neither of DJI's cameras is currently available in the US, which makes Insta360's Luna series a more compelling buy. Throw in great gimbal performance, excellent 4K footage, and, with the Luna Ultra, a zoom lens, and you have probably the best gimbal camera you can buy in the US.
Ultra Mega Pro
Insta360 launched the Luna Ultra in June. Looking like Wall-E, the Ultra features two lenses: one wide-angle main lens (developed with Leica) and one zoom lens. In September, Insta360 added the Luna Pro, which is largely identical to the Ultra but lacks the second zoom lens. Think of the Pro as the Ultra's budget-friendly version for those who don't mind sacrificing the zoom feature for cost savings.
The two cameras have more in common than they do different, so I'll highlight what they share before I get into what makes the Ultra a touch nicer than the Pro, and, for that matter, the DJI Osmo Pocket 4.
Both Luna models use a 20-mm equivalent lens with a wide, bright f/1.8 aperture. That main lens records to a 1-inch sensor, which means you're effectively shooting at the equivalent of a 20-mm f/5 lens on a full-frame (35-mm) camera.
The main sensor is the same 8K-capable 1-inch sensor found in the Insta360 X6 camera, but the Luna cameras deliver significantly better image quality because of the lens (or lenses, in the Ultra's case). In fact, the video from the Luna is vastly superior in almost every situation I tested, except in bright sunlight, where the Luna Ultra and X6 are roughly equivalent. The Luna's narrower field of view makes for sharper, clearer video. That 8K also means you can shoot with the main camera's digital 2X zoom and still get pretty dang nice 4K footage. On the other hand, the more durable X6 can handle shots you wouldn't want to risk with the more fragile Luna cameras, plus 360-degree photos and videos.
The Ultra's design mirrors what DJI has done for years with the Osmo Pocket series: a handle grip that houses most of the internals, a flip-out screen to turn it on, and a gimbal that holds the camera head at the top. It's a design that works well for filming both yourself and the world in front of you.
The three-axis gimbal not only keeps shots steady, but, as you'd expect, lets you smoothly pan, tilt, and roll without physically moving the entire camera or your body. You can set auto-tracking so the lens follows a subject automatically. The gimbal performed well in my testing, delivering stable shots. I occasionally had to recalibrate if I bumped or jarred it too much, but the process is quick and easy.
What sets Luna apart from the Osmo Pocket 4 is a detachable front panel with the OLED screen, buttons for record, zoom, and pan, plus a microphone. This means you can set up the camera and then use the screen remotely to frame yourself properly and control it from afar (up to approximately 66 feet, according to Insta360). This is extremely useful for anyone filming themselves.
The Luna cameras top out at 4K/120 frames per second (fps) for slow motion, which lags behind the Osmo Mobile 4's 4K/240 fps, but—and this is a big but—the Luna Ultra can shoot 4K/120 fps in log, whereas the Osmo Mobile cannot. If you color-grade and want slow motion, the Luna Ultra is the clear winner.
All of Insta360's advanced filming modes can be found in the Luna cameras, along with the usual color options, including the default 10-bit color profile and I-Log (Insta360's proprietary log format) recording for those who want to do their own color grading. In the default color profile, you can choose from about a dozen different filters. I find the default color mode oversaturated, especially in blue skies, which look extremely fake much of the time. I shoot almost exclusively with the Leica Natural color filter or in log and color-grade later.
Battery life seems pretty even for both Luna models. I recorded 4K/24-fps footage outdoors for two hours and 55 minutes. Ambient temps were about 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and I kept the camera out of direct sun for the test. The handle got pretty warm, but it didn't overheat. Even indoors, in a continuous shooting scenario like an interview, I don't think you'd have any issues with battery life or overheating on either camera. Sadly, the battery isn't replaceable, so you can't quickly swap one when it's dead. You can use a portable battery to keep it charged, but that makes the setup cumbersome.
Ultra Zoom
The Ultra's telephoto (zoom) lens uses a second but smaller 1/1.3-inch sensor. It has a 3X optical zoom (60-mm equivalent on a full-frame lens) but can reach up to 15X via digital zoom (300-mm equivalent). The Ultra launched with 12X digital zoom, but a firmware update increased it to 15X.
At first, I was somewhat underwhelmed by the zoom lens. If you're filming yourself (which I am loath to do, but never mind that), you don't need a zoom lens; the 20-mm is just about perfect. The zoom really comes in handy when shooting B-roll. Another scenario Insta360 touts is recording concerts or other live events from far away.
As you'd expect, image quality suffers considerably with the digital zoom. The processor does its best to keep the image sharp, but even in the best scenarios, the loss of quality is noticeable.
If your videos benefit from a zoom lens, consider the external zoom attachment Insta360 recently released, which adds 1.5X to the optical zoom (4.5X total), or the equivalent of a 90-mm lens. Unlike digital zoom, the image remains much sharper, but in my testing, I found almost no discernible loss of image quality when I used both optical and digital zoom with the telephoto attachment, at up to 200 mm. If you max out the digital zoom, you'll be shooting with the equivalent of a 450-mm lens, but the image does start to get softer.
When it launched, the Luna Pro featured 4K vertical video, while the Ultra did not. But now Insta360 has added 4K vertical video to the Ultra with a firmware update.
Over the Moon
First, who needs the Luna or the Osmo Pocket products? The target users include solo filmmakers, journalists, and content creators. That's why you often see them used by YouTubers and multimedia journalists.
Second, which Luna should you buy? The Luna Pro is probably the better value for most users. You do lose the zoom lens, but that's about it, and you save $170. The Ultra only makes more sense if you want to shoot with a longer focal length, but I don't think going beyond the 3X optical zoom is worthwhile.
If you're primarily interested in shooting yourself while moving—think walking, riding, skateboarding, etc.—it's also fair to consider Insta360's X6 in this equation. It can shoot similarly stable video by cropping its 360 footage. While both Luna cameras produce marginally better-looking video, the X6's 360-degree footage lets you pan around the shot in post, offering considerably more flexibility. Coupling the X6 with the folding selfie handle gives you an experience similar to the Luna. The X6 is also waterproof and virtually indestructible, so it can function as an action camera and 360 camera. To my mind, the main question is, do you need the higher-quality video of the Lunas? If you do, then the Luna cameras are the clear winner.
Finally, there's the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 and 4 Pro (the latter also called the 4P). Neither is officially for sale in the US, but you can find them on Amazon through third-party resellers. However, if registration, repair, support, and warranty matter to you, the Insta360 Luna series is your safer bet. If you want the absolute max dynamic range, the Osmo Pocket 4P boasts 17 stops of dynamic range and supports DJI's D-Log 2 log format. That's better dynamic range than all but one or two other cameras on the market. If that's what you're after, there's no competition, though remember color grading will crush much of that range anyway.
Beyond dynamic range, the Luna and Osmo Pocket cameras are pretty evenly matched, and since only one is officially available in the US, this is an easy choice.

articles.title: ‘Now they kiss my ass’: Trump on calling Google about the Gulf
articles.text:
Donald Trump described his call to Google to a crowd at Northern Kentucky University on Saturday.
“I called Google, Google Maps. See, Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first. Now they kiss my ass.” Donald Trump, at a rally in Highland Heights, Kentucky
He was speaking at the university’s Truist Arena in Highland Heights, at a midterm rally for Republican candidates. In the rally video, he was listing what he said he could do now that he could not have done before. He said this was “a much more powerful term” and that he could “do stuff that’s unbelievable”.
He then turned to a second name change. He said he had also renamed a lake in Canada as Lake America, referring to Lake Ontario.
What Google says
Google renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America on its maps last year. In August, it began labelling Lake Ontario as Lake America for US users. That came two days after Trump signed an executive order on the name.
Google said in a blog post at the time that it updates Maps to reflect name changes in “official government sources”. For the US, that source is the Geographic Names Information System. Google said the update followed its long-standing policy for bodies of water whose names vary from country to country.
Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge, which reported Trump’s remarks on Sunday.
Apple Maps also renamed the lake for US users in September. MapQuest refused to make the change.
